$comment: Cross-cutting infrastructure subsystem: the utilities, buildings, factories, energy and logistics that make every other subsystem possible. Depth 6-10 levels below facility.power etc., ending at things you could dig out of the ground or draw air from.

shared.facility.electricity: Grid supply arriving at a single factory: HV service -> substation -> step-down transformer -> LV bus -> motor control centre -> machine. Any subsystem that needs 'mains power' for a machine, a press or a test rig should reference this. Attach it with `from`, never `children` (CHECKLIST 1a).
shared.facility.water: Water chain for a plant: raw intake -> clarification -> filtration -> demineralisation -> RO/DI, plus the ordinary industrial side (cooling towers, evaporative cooling, process water). Two targets live below it and are the right ones to point at: facility.water.industrial for ordinary service water, facility.water.ultrapure for fab rinse water. Attach with `from`, never `children`.

facility.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen supply
facility.nitrogen.description: The single largest bulk gas. Used for inerting storage tanks and vessels, blanketing, purging, and as the carrier gas in diffusion furnaces and plasma etchers. Small plants bought a few tonnes a month of liquid N2. A furnace-loaded fab wanted tens of tonnes a day and built its own ASU.

children.name: Cryogenic air separation unit (ASU)
children.description: Air is filtered, compressed in a large multi-stage compressor to about 6-7 bar, cooled against the cold product streams until it liquefies, then fractionally distilled in a low-temperature column to make oxygen and a nitrogen-argon mixture. A unit also making argon has a separate argon column fed from the top of the nitrogen column. Typical small unit: 1,000-5,000 Nm3/h of oxygen.

facts.label: Oxygen delivery pressure
facts.value: typically 0.5-0.6 MPa at the battery limit, piped up to 3-4 MPa

children.note: Oxygen delivery pressure is the one number that gets conflated: 4000-6000 kPa is the high-pressure liquid-oxygen case, pumped at 50-100 bar before the warm end of the vaporiser, while a plant that piped oxygen directly would normally run at 400-600 kPa. Not established: the 1,000-5,000 Nm3/h small-unit size and the oxygen delivery pressures as figures. The air separation article describes the cycle and the high- and low-pressure columns. It gives no delivery pressure and no unit size.

children.name: PSA / molecular-sieve nitrogen generator
children.description: Pressure swing adsorption: compressed air is adsorbed on beds of zeolite molecular sieve at 7-10 bar, then dropped to near atmospheric and purged with a slice of product to release the nitrogen. Gave 90-99% nitrogen cheaply at small scale; the 1980s workhorse for factories of under a few hundred kW load.
children.note: Oxygen-enrichment PSA exists as a separate practice; the 4-6 MPa liquid-oxygen and high-pressure-pipeline conventions belong to the cryogenic branch, not to this one. Not established: the 90-99% nitrogen output and the 7-10 bar operating pressure. The pressure swing adsorption article documents the mechanism and the adsorbents (zeolite, activated carbon, silica gel, alumina, synthetic resins) but states no product purity or pressure.

children.name: Membrane nitrogen generator
children.description: Hollow-fibre asymmetric polyimide or cellulose acetate membranes in a pressure vessel, 20-40 bar feed, with N2 diffusing through the wall faster than O2. Cheap, silent, no regeneration heat, and limited to about 90-95% nitrogen, which is fine for blanketing and not fine for a furnace. By 1983 membrane units were new and uncommon. They took the small-plant market from PSA in the 1990s.
children.note: Not established: the 90-95% purity ceiling, the 20-40 bar feed pressure, and that membrane units were new and uncommon by 1983 and took the small-plant market from PSA only in the 1990s. Membrane separation is documented as an alternative to cryogenic air separation. The numbers and the dated market history are not.

children.name: Bulk cryogenic liquid storage
children.description: A double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless tank on a skirt, with a vacuum-insulated transfer line (a double pipe with perlite or multilayer reflective insulation between) from the ASU or the delivery tanker. The tank is a pressure vessel rated to about 700-1000 kPa on the inner shell.

facts.label: Tank sizes
facts.value: 5-60 m3 merchant tankers; 50-500 m3 on-site bulk tanks

children.note: Not established: the 700-1000 kPa inner-shell rating, the perlite or multilayer insulation detail, and the 5-60 m3 tanker and 50-500 m3 on-site tank sizes. No cryogenic tank standard was located.

facility.nitrogen.note: Not established: the three purity grades quoted (99.9% roughing, 99.99% blanketing, 99.999% furnace) and the tonnage split between small plants and a furnace-loaded fab.

facility.argon.name: Argon
facility.argon.description: Argon is not made. It is separated out. It is the third component of air and comes off the top of the ASU's nitrogen column, either as an argon-nitrogen mixture from a simple unit or as 99.99% pure from a dedicated argon column. Most 1980s plants bought it by the tanker as a by-product of someone else's oxygen plant.
facility.argon.note: Not established: that most 1980s plants bought argon by the tanker as a by-product of someone else's oxygen plant, and the 99.99% typical purity. The 0.93% abundance in air is the standard figure.

facility.helium.name: Helium
facility.helium.description: In 1983 helium was a genuinely scarce, genuinely odd commodity. Most of the world's supply came from a handful of natural-gas fractionation plants in Texas, Wyoming, Kansas and New Mexico, which extracted the 0.0005-0.005% helium in the gas as a crude 50-75% mixture. The rest came from four dedicated underground helium fields. These were the hug gas of Amarillo, Texas, and the Dixon and Harley fields in Kansas. Cryogenic separation of helium from LNG did not become industrial until the late 1990s.
facility.helium.note: Helium was rationed and price-controlled in the US until the 1996 helium policy change. A factory that needed it in 1983 wrote to a supplier, waited, and paid whatever was quoted. Not established: the helium content of natural gas quoted here (0.05-0.5 vol%, and 0.0005-0.005% in the description) and the 50-75% crude purity. Reference sources give helium in natural gas as up to several per cent by volume in the richest fields, which does not support these figures either way. Also not established: that cryogenic separation of helium from LNG did not become industrial until the late 1990s. Cryogenic separation from natural gas was in commercial use from the 1920s, and no source was located that dates LNG-based recovery as claimed.

children.name: Hug gas from an underground helium reservoir
children.description: The Permian Basin of west Texas and the southwest Kansas gas fields hold helium that never migrated out of the crust, trapped under impermeable salt and anhydrite since geological time. These are drilled specifically for helium, at tiny volumes. Amarillo field production was only tens of millions of cubic feet a year even in its peak.

facts.label: Fields
facts.value: Cliffside, Amarillo and Bush, Texas; Hugoton, Kansas

facts.label: Age of the source
facts.value: helium accumulated since Precambrian radiogenic decay

children.note: Partly established: the Cliffside field near Amarillo, Texas and the Bushton, Kansas connection are documented. Not established: the field list (Cliffside, Amarillo and Bush in Texas; Hugoton in Kansas), the Dixon, Kansas place entry, the Precambrian radiogenic accumulation as the age of the specific source, and the claim that Amarillo production was only tens of millions of cubic feet a year at peak.

shared.facility.steam: Industrial steam plant: coal- or oil-fired water-tube boilers, turbo-alternator, HP/LP header, condensate return, lime-soda and demineralised feedwater.
shared.facility.compressed-air: Instrument air and plant air: compressor, aftercooler, separator, dryer, receiver, ring main at 6-7 bar, plus nitrogen purge.

facility.coal.name: Steam coal (run-of-mine to sized)
facility.coal.description: The fuel. Bituminous coal, 20-35 GJ/t, 0.5-3% sulphur, bought on the international steam coal market or delivered by rail from the field. Its ash and sulphur content set the flue-gas desulphuriser and the bottom-ash grinder bill.

children.name: Coal mine
children.description: In 1983 the relevant supply was room-and-pillar underground mining in the Appalachian basin (Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky) for the US East Coast grid, and open-pit truck-and-shovel or bucket-wheel in the Powder River Basin, Silesia, the Ruhr, the Bowen Basin and the Witbank coalfield.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: typically 150-600 m underground in the Appalachians

children.note: Not established: that the 1983 US East Coast grid coal feeding the C64 supply came specifically from Appalachian room-and-pillar mines at 150-600 m depth, or from the listed Powder River, Silesian, Ruhr, Bowen Basin and Witbank sources. The basins and methods are generic industry description without a source tying them to this supply.

children.name: Coal preparation plant
children.description: Crushed, screened, washed and dried at the mine mouth. 1980s plants were dense-medium washers plus hydrocyclones. The resulting 2-inch x 0 coal with 8-12% moisture is what a boiler of that era was designed to burn. Thermal drying was the last step. A screen-deck or flash dryer brought the fuel down to about 8-12% moisture, because wetter coal burns slower, raises stack temperature and can quench a boiler screen tube.
children.note: Not established: that 1980s plants were dense-medium washers plus hydrocyclones, and the 8-12% product moisture figure and 2-inch x 0 top size. The encyclopaedia has no article on coal preparation (the title does not exist), and no coal preparation manual was located.

facility.coal.note: Established: bituminous coal as the steam-coal fuel, with an energy density around 24 GJ/t and sulphur of order 1-4%, consistent with the cited article's figures. Not established: the 20-35 GJ/t and 0.5-3% bands as quoted, and the market and rail procurement detail.

facility.oil.name: Crude petroleum and fuel oil
facility.oil.description: The liquid fuel of the whole industrial world in 1983. Kuwait and Saudi Arabian Light for the Far East, plus North Sea Brent and US domestic crude for Europe and the US East Coast.

children.name: Oil and gas well
children.description: A rotary or cable-tool hole completed into sandstone or carbonate. In 1983 the Far East's oil was largely onshore (Gawair in Kuwait, Ghawar-equivalent fields) with growing offshore production.

children.name: Refinery
children.description: Atmospheric and vacuum distillation plus hydrotreating to make fuel oil and, in a complex refinery, the naphtha feed for the hydrogen and ethylene crackers. Ali Qaido in Kuwait (1945) or Amuay in Venezuela (1962) typified the scale.

shared.facility.cleanroom: The semiconductor fab building: raised floor and plenum, HEPA filtration, laminar-flow ceiling, Class 100 / Class 1000 zoning, amber (yellow) photoresist room, air-change rate, and the operator population.

facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.name: Acetylene cylinder
facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.description: Dissolved acetylene at 15 bar in a porous monolithic mass (calcium carbide + acetone), in a steel shell. Calcium carbide came from the electric arc furnace carbide plant, i.e. ultimately from coal coke and quicklime.
facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.note: Not established: the 15 bar filling pressure and the porous monolithic calcium-carbide-and-acetone mass. The acetylene article confirms acetylene solubility in acetone and that calcium carbide production needs an electric arc furnace. The cylinder charging pressure is not stated in the text read.

facility.electricity.distribution-busbar.name: Busbar trunking and cable
facility.electricity.distribution-busbar.description: Copper or aluminium busbar in an epoxy-impregnated sandwich ('busway') for high-current runs, and PVC/PVDF-insulated copper or aluminium cable in conduit or tray for the rest. Flexible conduit was still common above machine tools.

facility.water.chem-treatment.name: Cooling-water chemical treatment
facility.water.chem-treatment.description: Chromate-based corrosion inhibitors (the dominant, and environmentally toxic, 1980s chemistry), or the newer phosphate/phosphonate/zinc formulations, plus biocide (chlorine or an organomercurial/isothiazolinone blend) and an antiscalant acid. This is where a large share of the plant's chemical consumption went.
facility.water.chem-treatment.note: Chromate inhibitors were being phased out across the industrial West in the 1980s. The same decade Commodore's own site was a Superfund listing because of chlorinated solvent handling.

facility.electricity.earthing.name: Earthing grid and lightning protection
facility.electricity.earthing.description: Copper rod or bare conductor bonded under the floor and up the steelwork, plus air terminals and down conductors to earth rods. The grid is not decoration: it is the reference for every protective device on the switchboard, and in a fab with a raised floor the earth grid and the electrostatic-dissipative floor were often the same conductor, bonded to the pedestals.
facility.electricity.earthing.note: Established by the cited articles: that a grounding or earthing electrode is a piece of conducting material buried in the soil, connected to equipment by a grounding electrode conductor, and that the purpose of connecting a system to the physical ground is to limit the voltage imposed by lightning events and by contact with higher-voltage lines; that the Earth serves as a reference against which other potentials are measured; and that the same type of ground applies to lightning protection systems. Not established: copper rod bonded under the floor and up the steelwork, air terminals with down conductors to earth rods, and the claim that in a fab with a raised floor the earth grid and the electrostatic-dissipative floor were the same conductor bonded to the pedestals; the sources describe electrode and bonding practice but not this installation detail.

facility.water.ultrapure.name: Ultrapure water
facility.water.ultrapure.description: The water that rinses a silicon wafer between every process step, and the water in which the thermal oxide grows. Target in 1983 was 10-15 MOhm-cm (roughly 1 ppb total ionic impurities) held at 20-25 C, distributed in 304 stainless or PVDF-lined piping. The yellow-lit photolithography bay and the wet chemical benches were the biggest consumers. The C64 itself was an assembly operation, not a fab, but every IC on its board came from a plant running exactly this chain. A modern practice note: the same chain now ends with UV and ultrafiltration, not with a mixed bed.

facts.label: 1983 practice
facts.value: 10-18 MOhm-cm; modern fabs specify 18 MOhm-cm at 25 C as a minimum

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: TOC <5 ppb in modern practice; 1980s practice often 50-100 ppb

facility.water.industrial.name: Ordinary industrial water
facility.water.industrial.description: The 99% of the plant's water use: cooling, washing, rinsing, boiler feed, human use. Deliberately not ultrapure, deliberately recycled. This branch is what a factory that needs cooling towers, a degreasing line or boiler make-up should point at. It draws the same raw intake as the ultrapure plant. Everything the plant throws away comes back through two routes: acid, solvent and dump rinses are collected, neutralised, filtered and returned to the pretreatment inlet (water conservation in a 1983 fab was a cost decision, not an environmental one, and a mature plant typically recovered 50-70% of its demand) while the liquid that could not be reclaimed was neutralised, settled and, where the acidity and fluoride demanded it, lime-neutralised with fluoride precipitation, then discharged to a municipal sewer under a permit or to an outfall.

facts.label: Reclaim recovery
facts.value: 50-70% of plant demand in a mature 1980s plant

facility.water.industrial.note: Not established: that a mature 1980s plant typically recovered 50-70% of its water demand, and the description of the fluoride-precipitation discharge route. Water reuse of that order is plausible industrial practice but no document states it.

facility.gases.oxygen.name: Oxygen supply
facility.gases.oxygen.description: Supplied as liquid oxygen from a merchant AS U or from the site unit. Used for the oxy-acetylene flame of the mechanical and maintenance shops, the gas-shielded welding of the metal frames, and increasingly for the oxygen plasma strip in a fab.
facility.gases.oxygen.note: Not established: the 99.6% industrial grade figure and the oxygen plasma strip use in fabs. Air separation units producing 97.5-99.5% oxygen are documented. Merchant liquid oxygen grades are not.

facility.gases.hydrogen.name: Hydrogen
facility.gases.hydrogen.description: Three routes in 1983: (a) bulk hydrogen from a merchant plant by tube trailer or by liquefaction; (b) on-site steam methane reforming of natural gas, the standard for anything above about 100 Nm3/h; and (c) electrolysis of demineralised water for the last, and highest, purity.
facility.gases.hydrogen.note: Not established: the 100 Nm3/h threshold above which steam methane reforming was the standard, and the 95% reformer / 99.99% electrolytic purity pair. Steam methane reforming as the cheapest source of industrial hydrogen is documented. The sizes and purities are not.

facility.gases.carbon-dioxide.name: Carbon dioxide (dry ice)
facility.gases.carbon-dioxide.description: Used in the plant for refrigerant cargo, for the dry-ice shipping of perishables, and (in the electronics plant) for nothing much; the two dry-ice applications in a 1980s C64 supply chain were chilling the shipped goods and cleaning moulds of frost. A large part of the 1980s merchant supply came not from an oil refinery but from hydrogen- and ammonia-based fertiliser plants, where the shift-reactor CO2 was captured and dried. It ends at natural gas and air.
facility.gases.carbon-dioxide.note: Established by the cited article: that carbon dioxide is a by-product of the industrial production of hydrogen by steam reforming and of the water gas shift reaction in ammonia production, both processes beginning with water and natural gas; and that liquid and solid carbon dioxide are important refrigerants in the food industry, employed during the transportation and storage of frozen foods, with solid carbon dioxide, called dry ice, used for small shipments where refrigeration equipment is not practical. Not established: that a large part of the 1980s merchant supply came from fertiliser plants with shift-reactor CO2 captured and dried, the dry-ice cleaning of moulds, the claim that the electronics plant had no real use for it, and the inputs listed here. The article names hydrogen and ammonia as sources but gives no share and no date for merchant supply in the 1980s.

facility.steam.styrene.name: Styrene monomer
facility.steam.styrene.description: Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene or by cracking benzene, both from the aromatic fraction of an oil refinery. A C8H8 molecule. This is the same feedstock family as the styrene in the ABS case of the C64.

facility.steam.asbestos.name: Asbestos (chrysotile) mineral
facility.steam.asbestos.description: Fibrous magnesium silicate mined from open pits and shafts in Quebec, South Africa, Italy and the Soviet Union, and spun, carded and woven into rope, cloth and board. This is the single most under-acknowledged raw material in any 1980s industrial plant.

children.name: Asbestos mine and mill
children.description: A serpentinite or chrysotile orebody worked by open pit or underground, then crushed, graded and carded. Ends at the serpentinite rock in the ground.

facility.steam.briquette.name: Coal briquette (hongsha / pressed coal)
facility.steam.briquette.description: Binderless or starch-bound anthracite fines pressed at 200 bar into egg-shaped briquettes about 100 g each, fired on a grate. Hong Kong's thermal power and much of its industrial boiler load ran on exactly this fuel.
facility.steam.briquette.note: Not established: the 200 bar pressing pressure, the 100 g egg-shaped briquette and the claim that Hong Kong's industrial boiler load ran on this fuel. The encyclopaedia has no article on coal briquettes, and no Hong Kong fuel document was located.

facility.coal.magnetite-ore.name: Magnetite ore body
facility.coal.magnetite-ore.description: Magnetite is rare as a bulk ore and common as a concentrates: the dense-medium coal washer only needs a few grams of Fe3O4 per litre of circulating slurry, so the ore was mined in small tonnages (often lake-shore or gabbro deposits) and concentrated by flotation and magnetic separation. Ends at the ore body in the ground.
facility.coal.magnetite-ore.note: The cited article describes magnetite as one of the main iron ores, which sits against this node's framing of magnetite as rare as a bulk ore. Not established: the small-tonnage lake-shore or gabbro deposits, the flotation plus magnetic-separation concentration, or any mine feeding this supply.

facility.steam.anthracite.name: Anthracite fines
facility.steam.anthracite.description: Hard, high-carbon coal, largely imported to the Far East from South Wales, Vietnam and China. Ends at the anthracite seam.
facility.steam.anthracite.note: Established by the cited article: anthracite as a hard, compact variety of coal with the highest carbon content, the fewest impurities and the highest energy density of all coals; the South Wales anthracite field lying west of Swansea and Llanelli; China mining more than three-quarters of world anthracite output and Vietnam among the principal producing countries; and that anthracite is divided by size, with fines below 10 mm going to sintering and pelletising. Not established: the Far East import flow, the Hon Gai and Pingxiang sources, and the use of anthracite fines as boiler fuel for the stations feeding this supply. The article says the principal use of anthracite is domestic heating and that its high value makes it prohibitively expensive for power plant use, and it names sintering and pelletising, not steam raising, as the fines applications.

facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.name: Atmospheric air
facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.description: 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, plus water and CO2. The single source of every bulk industrial gas. Delivered to an ASU intake through a windowless, acoustically baffled multi-bay intake so it arrived at a steady temperature, humidity and free of the dust that would plug a cryogenic plant.

children.name: Air intake stack
children.description: A tall concrete or brick stack with louvres facing away from the prevailing wind, feeding a plenum and the air compressor. Intakes were sited so that no two of them (for air, for cooling water, for the coal yard) were close enough to contaminate each other.
children.note: Not established: the concrete or brick stack with louvres, the plenum, the era, and the siting rule that no two intakes (for air, for cooling water, for the coal yard) were close enough to contaminate each other. No plant-layout, intake-design or siting document was located. The node describes a generic arrangement without a source.

facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.note: CO2 figure uncertain: the quoted 0.03% is the pre-1990 concentration. The standard reference composition of dry air gives carbon dioxide as 0.04%. The nitrogen, oxygen and argon figures are the standard 78.08 / 20.95 / 0.93%.

facility.water.aquifer.name: Confined sand-and-gravel aquifer
facility.water.aquifer.description: The buried glacial outwash and alluvial gravel bed, laid down in the Pleistocene and now saturated under pressure by an impermeable cap. It is the rock the well is drilled into, the source of the hardness and dissolved iron that the treatment plant has to remove, and the reason groundwater was preferred over river water for an ultrapure plant. Ends at the ground.
facility.water.aquifer.note: Not established: the Pleistocene age and glacial origin of the buried outwash the node describes, and the claim that groundwater was preferred over river water for an ultrapure plant. The aquifer article supports the confined-aquifer concept only.

facility.water.chromite.name: Chromite ore (FeCr2O4)
facility.water.chromite.description: The only economic source of chromium. Mined by underground stoping in the Bushveld Complex of South Africa and elsewhere, then smelted to ferrochrome.

children.name: Chromite mine
children.description: A stratiform chromite seam (UG2 in the Bushveld) worked by stoping or by open pit. Ends at the chromitite layer in the ground.

facility.water.di-loop.name: Ultrapure distribution loop
facility.water.di-loop.description: Slotted 316L stainless or PVDF-lined pipework in a continuous recirculating loop, running hot at 60-80 C to suppress bacteria, with take-off points at each wet bench. A loop that is not constantly moving will grow biofilm within a day. This was the single hardest problem in 1980s ultrapure water. Modern fabs add a terminal ultrafiltration barrier here (1-100 nm hollow-fibre membranes at 1-4 bar, stripping colloids, bacteria and endotoxin). In the 1980s the state of the art was a 0.2 micrometre-rated PTFE or nylon cartridge on the last loop, or nothing at all, and the loop ran hot instead. The liquid leaving the plant is the 10-15 MOhm-cm water the wet benches are plumbed to.

facts.label: Loop temperature
facts.value: 60-80 C (1980s practice); 20-25 C (modern practice, with UV/UF)

facility.water.di-loop.note: Modern fabs run the loop cold and sterilise it. Running hot was the 1980s answer to bio-growth. Not established: the 60-80 C hot-loop practice, the 10-15 Mohm-cm offtake figure, and the terminal ultrafiltration comparison for 1980s plants. No document was located on 1980s ultrapure water distribution loop temperature.

facility.water.pvdf.name: PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride)
facility.water.pvdf.description: A fluoropolymer from vinylidene fluoride, chemically inert to ultrapure water and to most process acids, used as a liner or as solid pipe in ultrapure service. Melting point about 177 C, and it will not support microbial growth.
facility.water.pvdf.note: Not established: the claim that PVDF will not support microbial growth. The PVDF article supports its origin by polymerising vinylidene difluoride and its non-reactive character, and gives the melting point as 177 C.

facility.water.pp.name: Polypropylene piping
facility.water.pp.description: Polypropylene was the cheapest acid- and chemical-resistant pipe for wet-bench waste lines and reclaim, and (as spun-bonded fabric) the material of the 1980s 'class 100' air filter pre-filter.
facility.water.pp.note: Not established: that polypropylene was the cheapest acid-resistant pipe for 1980s wet-bench waste lines, or that spun-bonded polypropylene was the standard air-filter pre-filter material of the decade.

facility.electricity.askarel.name: Askarel (PCB-filled transformer dielectric)
facility.electricity.askarel.description: A chlorinated biphenyl dielectric used from the 1930s until the 1980s ban. Ends at the chlorinated benzene/aromatics stream.
facility.electricity.askarel.note: Established by the cited article: askarel as a trade name under which PCBs were sold in the United Kingdom and the United States alongside Aroclor and Asbestol; the dielectric utility of PCBs resting on chemical stability, low flammability and high dielectric constant; insulating fluid for transformers and capacitors as a closed application; commercial production from 1929 under Swann Chemical and taken over by Monsanto in 1935; and the United States ban on domestic production under the Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976, effective January 1, 1978, with enclosed uses such as transformer insulating fluid allowed to remain in service. Not established: a 1980s end date. The legislation and its effective date in the source are 1976 and 1978, and the article separately dates commercial production bans to 1979, all earlier than the 1980s this node closes on. Also not established: the chlorobenzene and biphenyl feedstock route, which the article does not cover.

facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.name: Chlorinated aromatic feedstock
facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.description: Chlorobenzene and biphenyl feedstock for the askarel blend, itself from the chlorination of benzene over a chloride catalyst. Ends at the aromatic hydrocarbon still.
facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.note: Not verified for a specific 1980s askarel producer. Era caveat: US PCB production for askarel halted in 1977 with the TSCA ban effective 1978-79, so a 1983 chlorobenzene feed reads as legacy in-service fluid or non-US make, not current US production.

facility.cleanroom.silica.name: High-purity silica
facility.cleanroom.silica.description: The same raw material as the fused-quartz diffusion tube, the photomask substrate and the ceramic package: high-purity SiO2. In 1983 most came from Brazil or from the US inland deposit, and by the mid-80s the industry moved to synthetic vapour-deposited silicon tetrafluoride because natural high-purity quartz was getting scarce.

facility.hazardous-waste.tce-feedstock.name: Ethylene from the steam cracker
facility.hazardous-waste.tce-feedstock.description: The chlorination of ethylene, or the oxychlorination of 1,2-dichloroethane, which is itself from the chlorination of ethylene. The ethylene came from naphtha steam cracking. This is the same petrochemical chain as everything else on this tree. Ends at the crude oil still.

facility.hazardous-waste.spent-acid.name: Spent acid and alkali
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-acid.description: Sulfuric and hydrochloric acid exhausted by the etchers and the wet benches, plus the caustic and the alkaline develop and strip baths. Neutralised with lime into a metal hydroxide sludge; the arsenic-containing liquor from the diffusion furnaces went the same way.
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-acid.note: Not established: that the diffusion furnaces' arsenic-containing liquor was neutralised into the same hydroxide sludge stream. No document was located on 1980s semiconductor arsenic waste handling.

facility.hazardous-waste.spent-solvent.name: Spent organic solvent and resist stripper
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-solvent.description: Acetone, xylene, toluene, isopropanol and cellosolve acetate from the degreasers, plus the spent developer (tetramethylammonium hydroxide from positive photoresist) and stripper from the coat-develop track. Recovered by activated-carbon adsorption and distillation where that was economical, and otherwise vapour-incinerated.
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-solvent.note: Not established: that tetramethylammonium hydroxide developer and cellosolve acetate stripper were the specific 1980s resist-track waste streams, and that activated-carbon recovery was preferred for cost reasons even in 1983. No document was located for the photolithography waste chemistry of that decade.

facility.hazardous-waste.plating-rinse.name: Cyanide- and metal-bearing plating rinse
facility.hazardous-waste.plating-rinse.description: Rinse water carrying gold, tin, copper, nickel and chromium out of the plating line. The cyanide-bearing stream needed alkaline chlorination before discharge. The acid-bearing stream went to the neutralisation tank. Both ended up in the same hydroxide sludge.

facility.power.uranium-ore.name: Uranium ore (U3O8)
facility.power.uranium-ore.description: Graded and leached in the 1970s-80s, largely from the Colorado Plateau (Uravan) and New Mexico, plus Namibia and Canada. Ends at the orebody.
facility.power.uranium-ore.note: Established: uranium ore as the mined feedstock, extraction by open pit, underground mining or in-situ leaching, and the near-total use of mined uranium as reactor fuel. Not established: that the ore feeding this supply was graded and leached in the 1970s-80s, or that it came from Uravan on the Colorado Plateau, from New Mexico, from Rossing in Namibia and from Canada. No mine or mill document was located for any of these places or for the flowsheet described.

facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore.name: Vanadiferous uraninite ore
facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore.description: The US Colorado Plateau ore, carnotite, carried vanadium as well as uranium: carnotite was first mined in the Uravan Mineral Belt from 1898, and vanadium was recovered alongside uranium as a by-product rather than being separable from it. The documented recovery route roasts the crushed ore with sodium chloride or sodium carbonate at about 850 C to give sodium metavanadate, whose aqueous extract is acidified to red cake and reduced with calcium metal.
facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore.note: Corrected: the chlorine leach and the salt-roast soda-ash-leach flowsheet previously given here are both wrong as stated. Vanadium metal production begins with roasting crushed ore with sodium chloride or sodium carbonate at about 850 C to give sodium metavanadate. The aqueous extract of that solid is acidified to give red cake, a polyvanadate salt, which is reduced with calcium metal. Carnotite was the Colorado Plateau ore, first mined in the Uravan Mineral Belt from 1898, and it carried vanadium as well as uranium, so vanadium came out as a by-product of uranium production. Confidence stays medium because which of the two the mills serving this supply ran principally for is not established, and no plant-level document for the 1983 route was found. An earlier citation to the Colorado Geological Survey study was withdrawn: it is a 164-page PDF that could not be read end to end in this environment, so its wording was second-hand.

facility.power.iron-ore.name: Blast furnace iron ore
facility.power.iron-ore.description: The blast-furnace feed, and the reason a power station's turbine steel has a supply chain at all. US supply was Mesabi Range hematite and taconite in the Lake Superior district, shipped by rail to the blast furnaces of the Great Lakes steel belt. Europe and Japan imported Brazilian pellets and ore. Ends at the orebody.

children.name: Iron ore open pit (Mesabi)
children.description: Taconite and hematite are dug by 15-tonne payload shovels and hauled in 90-tonne trucks from a strip 60 m deep. Ends at the orebody.

facility.power.coking-coal-seam.name: High-Bituminous coking coal seam
facility.power.coking-coal-seam.description: A very specific subset of bituminous coal. This is the seam that swells and fuses in the coke oven, distinct from the steam coal the power station burns. The Pennsylvania/Kentucky/West Virginia 'High Bituminous' field.
facility.power.coking-coal-seam.note: Established by the cited article: coking coal is the grade that produces good coke for the blast furnace. Not established: the swelling-and-fusing High Bituminous seam characterisation, or the Connellsville, Kuznetsk and Ruhr places, for the coke feeding this supply.

facility.steam.ion-resin.name: Ion-exchange resin (polystyrene-DVB)
facility.steam.ion-resin.description: A gel-type cation resin (sulfonic acid groups) or an anion resin (quaternary ammonium groups) on a cross-linked polystyrene-divinylbenzene bead. Beads of 0.3-1.0 mm, sieved into size fractions so the fine resin could be kept out of the top of the bed.

facility.steam.hardness-sludge.name: Calcium carbonate / magnesium hydroxide sludge
facility.steam.hardness-sludge.description: The lumpy waste from lime-soda softening, pumped to a thickener and then to a drying bed or trucked to landfill wet. This is the sludge that fills the lagoons around old steel and chemical works.

facility.coal.magnetite.name: Magnetite sand
facility.coal.magnetite.description: Fe3O4, a natural iron oxide sand used as the density medium because it is dense, cheap, recoverable magnetically and chemically inert.
facility.coal.magnetite.note: Established by the cited article: magnetite is Fe3O4, an iron oxide, ferrimagnetic and one of the main iron ores. Not established: that the dense-medium washers feeding this supply used natural magnetite sand specifically, or the iron-ore-concentrate input as its source.

facility.coal.overburden-strip.name: Overburden strip of shale and clay
facility.coal.overburden-strip.description: Burden stripped in benches to reach the coal seam. This was often 10-60 m of rock and dirt per metre of coal in the Powder River Basin. The overburden itself becomes a backfill and a landfill-pond liner.
facility.coal.overburden-strip.note: Not established: the 10-60 m of overburden per metre of Powder River coal, the benching method, or the reuse of stripped rock as backfill and pond liner for the mines feeding this supply; the figures and the Wyoming/Montana place carry no source.

facility.coal.room-pillar-seam.name: Seam between shale and sandstone beds
facility.coal.room-pillar-seam.description: The same Carboniferous coal-bearing sequence as the longwall face, mined from a shaft or slope rather than a portal. Ends at the rock in the ground.

facility.coal.seam.name: Bituminous coal seam in sedimentary rock
facility.coal.seam.description: The raw input, full stop. In the northern Appalachian basin the commercial coal is in the middle and upper Pennsylvanian (Conemaugh, Monongahela, Kittanning, Freeport) formations. This is Carboniferous, roughly 300 million years old, laid down in swamp forests and buried under Pennsylvanian sediment.

facility.water.chromate.name: Sodium chromate inhibitor
facility.water.chromate.description: A dichromate/chromate film former that passivates the steel of the cooling system. Enormously effective, and the reason thousands of 1980s cooling towers are a chromate source in the groundwater.
facility.water.chromate.note: Not established: that chromate was a film-forming corrosion inhibitor in cooling systems, and the claim about thousands of chromate-bearing cooling towers in the 1980s. The encyclopaedia article on sodium chromate is a bare formula page and states none of this.

facility.water.ro-membrane.name: Cellulose acetate / TFC membrane
facility.water.ro-membrane.description: A 0.2-1.5 micrometre-thick selective layer on a polysulphone support, wound into a spiral and potted with epoxy. This is the same membrane family as the 1541 floppy's read/write head gap in spirit (a nanoscale selective barrier) but the RO element was 1 m long.
facility.water.ro-membrane.note: Established by the cited article: that RO membranes are made in a variety of configurations with the two most common being spiral-wound and hollow-fibre; that current RO membranes are thin-film composite polyamide; that the spiral-wound design is engineered for one-way flow and does not allow backpulsing or air agitation to scour its surface; and that pretreatment is a necessity for any RO system. Not established: the cellulose acetate layer, the polysulphone support, the 0.2-1.5 micrometre selective-layer thickness, the epoxy potting, and the 1 m element length; the article names polyamide thin-film composite and hollow fibre but does not mention cellulose acetate or polysulphone, and states no layer thickness and no element length. The comparison with a read/write head gap is a figure of speech, not a measurement.

facility.water.filter-sand.name: Silica filter sand
facility.water.filter-sand.description: Washed, graded, nearly pure SiO2 sand with effective size 0.5-0.7 mm. A large, unglamorous, and genuinely scarce mineral input to any waterworks.

children.description: A pit worked by river dredging or by bank excavation beside a watercourse, screening the outwash into a concrete-aggregate fraction and a finer silica fraction. Filter sand is scarce: it has to be nearly pure SiO2 with an effective size of 0.5-0.7 mm, and most river gravel is too dirty to wash up to standard. Ends at the sand deposit.
children.name: Sand and gravel extraction pit
children.note: Not established: that filter sand is scarce because most river gravel is too dirty to wash up to standard. No document located.

facility.water.filter-sand.note: Not established: that filter sand has an effective size of 0.5-0.7 mm and that it is a scarce mineral input. The encyclopaedia has no article on filter or silica sand for water treatment (the Silica sand article redirects to sand casting), and no waterworks standard was located.

facility.water.anthracite.name: Anthracite filter coal
facility.water.anthracite.description: Hard, coarse anthracite crushed to 1-2 mm as the coarse top layer. Same material as the boiler fuel, just graded differently.
facility.water.anthracite.note: Not established: the 1-2 mm grading as a filter medium. Anthracite is documented as a hard, high-carbon coal used for power generation and metallurgy. Its use as crushed filter coal is not stated in the cited article.

facility.water.alum.name: Alum (hydrated aluminium sulfate)
facility.water.alum.description: The workhorse coagulant. Made from bauxite (or domestic low-grade bauxite/clay) digested in sulphuric acid and crystallised. Ended at the bauxite mine by way of the same chain that makes the aluminium in the grid conductor.

facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.name: Spun-bonded polypropylene
facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.description: Polypropylene melt-spun into continuous filaments and laid down in a random web, then bonded by heat or needle punching. Cheapest possible cleanroom garment material, and the raw material for the 'tacky mat' that caught shoe-borne particles at every airlock.
facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.note: Not established: that spun-bonded polypropylene was the standard 1980s cleanroom garment material or the standard tacky-mat material. Spun-bonded fabric has no separate encyclopaedia article, and no standard or industry document was located for this material in the cleanroom trade in that decade.

facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.name: Heavy-metal hydroxide sludge
facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.description: A wet, low-solids sludge of iron, aluminium, chromium, copper, nickel, zinc and cadmium hydroxides, filtered on a plate-and-frame or belt press to 15-25% solids and trucked to a hazardous landfill in a lined, covered cell. In 1983 this was the default destination and the reason so many US sites are now Superfund sites.
facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.note: Not established: the 15-25% solids figure after plate-and-frame or belt press dewatering, and the characterisation of lined covered cells as the default 1983 destination. The sludge composition claim is not sourced either.

facility.power.limestone.name: Limestone (calcium carbonate) slurry
facility.power.limestone.description: Crushed and slaked to calcium hydroxide for wet scrubbing, or used directly in dry/semi-dry scrubbers. Ends at the quarry.

facility.water.aquifer-gravel.name: Aquifer sand and gravel
facility.water.aquifer-gravel.description: Glacial outwash and alluvial gravel forming the confined aquifer; the raw material of the well itself and the source of the hardness and iron.
facility.water.aquifer-gravel.note: Not established: that the Lehigh Valley, Chianan Plain and Hong Kong aquifers are confined sand-and-gravel of Pleistocene age. Aquifers as a concept are sourced. The per-place geology is not.

facility.electricity.feldspar.name: Feldspar
facility.electricity.feldspar.description: A potassium-sodium aluminosilicate used as a flux in porcelain and in the electrolytic alumina bath. Ends at the pegmatite quarry.
facility.electricity.feldspar.note: Established by the cited article: feldspar as a group of aluminium tectosilicate minerals containing sodium, calcium or potassium, making up about 60 percent of the Earth crust; its use in the ceramic industry as a flux that forms a glassy phase in bodies during firing and promotes vitrification, and as a source of alkalies and alumina in glazes; and about 66 percent of United States consumption going to glassmaking, including glass fibre. Not established: the use in the electrolytic alumina bath, which the article does not mention, and the pegmatite quarry endpoint with the Pezzullo and North Carolina places; the article does describe pegmatites as very coarse igneous rock composed mainly of quartz, feldspar and mica, but ties no named quarry to this supply.

facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.name: Coarse glass-fibre filter media
facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.description: Glass melted and blown into coarse fibres and felted into a mat. The same glassfibre technology as the HEPA medium but 100-1000x coarser and far cheaper. Ends at the glass batch.

facility.cleanroom.hepa-glass-fibre.name: Borosilicate glass microfibre
facility.cleanroom.hepa-glass-fibre.description: Glass melted at 1400 C and blown into fibres a few micrometres across, then laid into a paper and fired at 800-900 C to set a bonding agent, and chopped into slivers. Every 1980s fab consumed tens of thousands of these filters a year and changed them on a schedule rather than on condition.

facility.power.kaolin.name: Kaolin (china clay)
facility.power.kaolin.description: A white kaolinite clay from a kaolin pit, washed and beneficiated for the ceramic and paper trades. Ends at the clay pit.

facility.oil.lpg.name: LPG (propane/butane)
facility.oil.lpg.description: The liquid the Hong Kong and Japanese industrial estates burned for process heat and factory heating, and the feedstock for the 1980s alkylation route to isobutylene. Ends at the well or the refinery.
facility.oil.lpg.note: Established: liquefied petroleum gas as the propane-and-butane mixture sold as a bulk fuel for industrial heat, and its origin at the gas field or as a refinery stream. Not established: that the Hong Kong and Japanese industrial estates feeding this supply burned LPG rather than town gas, fuel oil or kerosene, or that this LPG was the feedstock for an alkylation unit. The location and route claims carry no source.

facility.oil.reservoir.name: Sandstone or carbonate oil reservoir
facility.oil.reservoir.description: Porous sedimentary rock (typically Tertiary sandstone or Jurassic carbonate) saturated with oil under pressure. This is where the story actually ends for oil.
facility.oil.reservoir.note: Not established: that the reservoirs supplying the Far East trade of 1983 were typically Tertiary sandstone or Jurassic carbonate. No petroleum-geology document was located for these fields.

facility.steam.insulation.name: Steam pipe insulation
facility.steam.insulation.description: Moulded magnesium-block sections, calcium silicate or, on hot surfaces, an asbestos-based rope and canvas wrap. Asbestos lagging was utterly routine on a 1980s steam line and is the reason so many power and chemical plants have mesothelioma claims decades later.

facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide.name: Hollow-fibre polyimide membrane
facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide.description: A thin-walled asymmetric fibre, about 0.1-0.2 micrometre wall, with a selectively permeable outer skin. Making a defect-free fibre over a 1 m length was, and is, the hard part.
facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide.note: Established by the cited article: that hollow fibre membranes are made by extruding a polymer solution through the annulus of a spinneret, so that it retains a hollow cylindrical shape and solidifies, by wet, dry-jet wet, dry or melt spinning; that the fibres are then assembled in parallel into a module with the fibre ends fixed together in a resin or epoxy; and that a textbook on gas separation membranes is cited for those spinning methods. Not established: polyimide as the specific polymer, the 0.1-0.2 micrometre wall, the selectively permeable outer skin on an asymmetric fibre, and the claim that making a defect-free fibre over a 1 m length is the hard part; the article does not name polyimide, states no wall thickness and does not describe a fibre of that length.

facility.nitrogen.zeolite.name: Zeolite molecular sieve (synthetic)
facility.nitrogen.zeolite.description: Crystalline hydrated aluminosilicate with a uniform 3-5 angstrom pore, made by hydrothermal crystallisation of bentonite, kaolin or synthetic gels. Uniform aperture size is what makes PSA possible. A zeolite with 3A pores excludes N2 and adsorbs only O2 and H2O. The 4A and 5A grades are used elsewhere in gas drying.
facility.nitrogen.zeolite.note: The same chemistry gives the 4A sieve that fills the R-2400 filter's perforated shell in the C64's power supply, if the cartridge was the zeolite type rather than the coil type. Not established: the 3-5 angstrom pore size and the claim that a 3A pore excludes N2 while adsorbing O2 and water. The zeolite article confirms that the major molecular sieves 3A, 4A and 5A are all LTA type and defines molecular sieving by size exclusion. The pore figures and the selective-adsorption detail are not in it.

facility.hazardous-waste.generation.name: Spent acid, solvent and plating waste streams
facility.hazardous-waste.generation.description: The three physical waste streams that carried almost all of a 1980s electronics plant's hazardous load: the spent acids and alkalis from etching and cleaning, the spent organic solvents and resist stripper from photolithography and degreasing, and the cyanide- and metal-bearing rinses from gold and tin plating. Each was a bulk liquid, collected in a tank, and each needed its own treatment route. Small generators (which in 1983 was most of Commodore's Hong Kong subcontractor base) had almost no obligations at all beyond a monthly manifest.
facility.hazardous-waste.generation.note: Not established: that small generators such as Commodore's Hong Kong subcontractor base had almost no obligations beyond a monthly manifest in 1983. RCRA's small-quantity-generator rules are in the Subtitle C regime, and the number of copies on a manifest is set by regulation, not established here.

facility.power.acsr-conductor.name: Aluminium conductor steel-reinforced (ACSR)
facility.power.acsr-conductor.description: Aluminium strands around a steel core for tensile strength, twisted and stranded on the line. Ends at an aluminium smelter fed by alumina.
facility.power.acsr-conductor.note: Not established: the construction and the endpoint as stated. The encyclopaedia has no article on aluminium conductor steel-reinforced cable (the title does not exist). Aluminium strands around a steel core for tensile strength is generic industry practice, carried here with an ASTM B232 scope citation; the pre-1982 lineage of the composition is unverified.

facility.power.uranium.name: Uranium fuel
facility.power.uranium.description: Uranium concentrate converted to UF6 and enriched from natural 0.71% U-235 to 2.5-3.5%, then fabricated into ceramic UO2 pellets 8 mm across, sintered, ground to length, clad in zircaloy and made into a fuel assembly. In 1983 the US HEU was being phased down and the world's enrichment market was switching to centrifuge cascades.
facility.power.uranium.note: Established: the front end of the fuel cycle in general terms. This is concentrate converted to UF6, enriched by isotope separation, then fabricated into ceramic UO2 pellets, sintered, ground to length, clad in zircaloy and assembled into a fuel element. Not established: the 2.5-3.5 percent U-235 figure as a 1983 light-water-reactor enrichment, the 8 mm pellet diameter, or the claim that in 1983 US HEU was being phased down and the world enrichment market was switching to centrifuge cascades. No reactor fuel specification or 1983 enrichment-market document backs them here.

facility.power.river.name: River itself
facility.power.river.description: A glacial or monsoonal river carrying suspended sediment, hardness and organic colour. This is the actual origin of most of the ultrapure water in this tree.
facility.power.river.note: Not established: the named rivers and reservoirs and their characterisations, including Sun Moon Lake, the Sham Chun, the Han River basin, and the claim that this is the actual origin of most of the ultrapure water on the tree. No water authority document located.

facility.power.rockfill.name: Rockfill dam and riprap
facility.power.rockfill.description: Dams of the era were built of quarried rock tipped into the river and compacted, faced with concrete or asphaltic membrane. Ends at the quarry face.

children.name: Aggregate and riprap quarry
children.description: Granite/gneiss quarried, crushed and screened for dam rock, concrete aggregate and filter material. Ends at the rock in the hillside.
children.note: Not established: that granite or gneiss was quarried for dam rock, concrete aggregate and filter material in this supply chain. No quarry or aggregate statistics document was located.

facility.power.rockfill.note: Established by the cited article: an embankment dam is placed and compacted soil or rock with a water-resistant covering. Not established: that the dams behind the stations feeding this supply were quarried rock tipped into the river and compacted with concrete or asphaltic facing, or that the fill ended at a quarry face.

facility.power.cement-portland.name: Portland cement
facility.power.cement-portland.description: Limestone plus clay, fired in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, ground with gypsum. The universal structural binder of the 1980s industrial plant: dams, cooling towers, substation foundations, effluent tanks, the fab's raised floor.

facility.steam.fuel.name: Industrial boiler fuel
facility.steam.fuel.description: Anthracite, bituminous coal, fuel oil or (very commonly in Hong Kong, Japan and Taiwan) coal briquettes pressed from imported anthracite fines in a ring-die or pillow press.

facility.electricity.electrical-steel.name: Grain-oriented silicon steel (GOES)
facility.electricity.electrical-steel.description: 3.2% silicon steel rolled so its crystallographic grain lies parallel to the flux direction, giving a core loss an order of magnitude lower than hot-rolled steel. Made in a special continuous-annealing line. This is the same material used in the C64's switch-mode transformer and in every mains transformer in the world.
facility.electricity.electrical-steel.note: Deliberately stiff magnetically so it laminates easily and does not ring when punched. 'GOES' is stamped on the laminations.

children.name: Grain-oriented steel rolling mill
children.description: Hot band rolled to 2 mm, cold rolled to 0.3 mm, decarburised in a hydrogen atmosphere and given a final magnetic anneal. Ends at the ore and the coke oven.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that the carbon level in electrical steel is reduced by annealing the alloy in a decarburising atmosphere such as hydrogen, that increasing the average crystal size decreases hysteresis loss so that a final heat treatment can be applied to form a normal grain size of about 150 micrometres, and that the material is supplied as cold-rolled strip less than 2 mm thick, cut into laminations and stacked into transformer cores. Not established: hot band rolled to 2 mm and cold rolled to 0.3 mm as a gauge schedule, and a separate named final magnetic anneal; the source gives a sub-2 mm strip thickness and one general heat treatment, not the two-stage rolling path or the anneal by name.

facility.electricity.insulating-oil.name: Transformer insulating oil
facility.electricity.insulating-oil.description: Mineral oil (naphthenic or paraffinic), a by-product of vacuum distillation of crude. Also Askarel (PCB-filled chlorinated dielectric) in older units. This is a PCB source that explains part of the PCB contamination of the Hudson/Superfund sites.
facility.electricity.insulating-oil.note: Askarel transformers were phased out in the US after the EPA began classifying PCBs as hazardous in 1979. By 1983 new units were mineral-oil or dry-type.

facility.compressed-air.pvc-packing.name: PVC / PP packing media
facility.compressed-air.pvc-packing.description: Moulded plastic ring or saddle packing, chemically inert to acid and alkali where ceramic or metal would be attacked. The same vinyl chloride monomer chain that makes the conduit and the cable in the plant.

facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel.name: Nickel-alloy rotor and casing steel
facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel.description: For a 540 C steam turbine the high-pressure rotor needed 0.5-0.8% Cr-Mo-V steel and the last stages austenitic stainless. The whole thing was forged, normalised, stress-relieved and then creep-rupture proof-tested.
facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel.note: Not established: the 540 C steam condition, the 0.5-0.8 percent chromium-molybdenum-vanadium high-pressure rotor steel, the austenitic stainless last stages, or the forging, normalising, stress-relief and creep-rupture proof test for the turbines feeding this supply; the alloy and treatment carry no source.

facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.name: Oxy-acetylene flame
facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.description: Oxygen plus a locally generated acetylene from calcium carbide (in the Far East, imported cylinder acetylene was common). This is the flame that welded every sheet-metal chassis, rack and jig in the factory.
facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.note: Not established: that locally generated carbide acetylene was the practice in the Far East with imported cylinders common, and that this flame welded every sheet-metal chassis in the factory. Acetylene's use for welding and cutting is documented. The site practice is not.

facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming.name: Steam methane reforming
facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming.description: Natural gas is desulphurised to under 0.5 ppm sulphur, mixed with steam at 3:1 and passed over a nickel-molybdenum or chromite catalyst at 800-850 C and 15-25 bar. This gives hydrogen plus CO, and the CO is shifted over an iron-chrome catalyst to CO2 and more hydrogen. Then CO2 is removed by amine scrubbing or molecular sieve.
facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming.note: Established: steam methane reforming over a nickel catalyst at 800-900 C and 20-30 bar with a 2.5-3:1 steam-to-carbon ratio, plus the water-gas shift step, per the cited article. Not established: the under-0.5 ppm desulphurisation figure and the nickel-molybdenum/chromite and iron-chrome catalyst specifics.

facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.name: Electrolysis of demineralised water
facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.description: In a diaphragm or, from the 1970s, an alkaline cell, a nickel-plated or activated-titanium cathode makes hydrogen while a nickel anode makes oxygen. Fed with conductivity-grade water at 20-25 C. Output purity is 99.99% once the cell gas is passed over a palladium diffuser or an oxygen getter. This is the 'deoxo' step that killed the last 0.1% of oxygen.

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: about 50-55 kWh per kg of hydrogen

facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.note: Not established: the 50-55 kWh per kg energy figure, the nickel anode and activated-titanium cathode construction, the palladium diffuser deoxo step, and the 99.99% output purity. The electrolysis article confirms water electrolysis gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode and describes the palladium-diffusion problem. It does not state the specific cell chemistry or energy figure of that era.

facility.steam.condensate-return.name: Condensate return
facility.steam.condensate-return.description: Steam traps in every steam-consuming process returned hot condensate to the hotwell. Recovering it saved both fuel and water-treatment chemical, and the copper condensate pipework of a 1980s plant was a continuous, weeping mess of unions and gaskets.

children.name: Steam trap
children.description: A thermostatic (bimetallic or liquid-expansion) or mechanical bucket trap with a strainer upstream. Failed-open traps cost fuel. Failed-closed traps flooded the plant. Every steam system of the era leaked at a few percent of its steam load, largely from these.

facility.steam.feedwater-treatment.name: Boiler feedwater treatment
facility.steam.feedwater-treatment.description: Two chemistries: lime-soda softening for the low-pressure plant, and ion-exchange demineralisation for anything above about 20 bar. By 1983 the whole industry standard was sodium-cycle cation plus strong-base anion demineralisation with a mixed-bed polish.

children.name: Lime-soda softening
children.description: Slaked lime Ca(OH)2 and soda ash Na2CO3 are dosed into a hot reaction basin, converting the scale-forming calcium and magnesium hardness into calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide sludge, which settles in a clarifier. This is the classic 1900-1960 process, still running at small industrial plants in 1983. Produces a lot of sludge.

children.name: Burn and hydrate lime
children.description: Quicklime CaO is burnt from limestone in a vertical or flash calciner at about 1000 C, losing its carbon dioxide as CO2 and leaving a caustic porous solid. It is then hydrated, an exothermic reaction that turns it into slaked lime Ca(OH)2 for the lime-soda process. Ends at the limestone quarry face.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.56 t CaO per tonne of pure CaCO3

children.name: Ion-exchange demineralisation
children.description: A cation exchanger in the sodium form swaps Ca/Mg for Na; a strongly basic anion exchanger then swaps the bicarbonate/sulphate/chloride anions for OH; CO2 is degassed between the two beds by a packed or bubble column, because skipping the degasser overloaded the anion resin with carbonic acid and shortened its life; the effluent is then polished in a mixed bed to the sodium-chloride equivalent of a few tens of ppb. Resin is regenerated with 10-20% caustic and 6-12% hydrochloric or sulphuric acid, and each regeneration blew a large slug of acidic or alkaline brine once or twice a day that had to go somewhere. This was in 1983 usually a lined lagoon, a settling pond and then a discharge permit.

facts.label: Demineralised water
facts.value: typically 0.1-1.0 us/cm (10-100 Mohm-cm) after a mixed bed

facts.label: Regeneration frequency
facts.value: once or twice a day per bed

children.note: Modern practice adds a second pass of RO/mixed bed and typically achieves 18 Mohm-cm. The 1980s benchmark for a good mixed bed was 10-15 Mohm-cm.

facility.helium.cryo-separation.name: Cryogenic helium separation from natural gas
facility.helium.cryo-separation.description: The gas is chilled to -190 C through a train of plate-fin heat exchangers. Helium, having the second-lowest boiling point, stays in the vapour phase and is drawn off from the top of the cold box as a crude 50-75% helium stream. Then purified by cryogenic adsorption, catalytic dehydrogenation of the residual hydrogen and activated-carbon adsorption of the nitrogen. The last step adsorbs the nitrogen on a char bed at 77 K to give 99.995% (5N) or 99.9999% (6N) helium. The same activated-carbon adsorption principle as the water-treatment carbon, run at liquid-nitrogen temperature.

children.name: Liquid helium dewar (4.2 K)
children.description: A double-walled stainless vessel with a superinsulating vacuum jacket, holding 4.2 K liquid helium for a cryostat or a superconducting magnet. Expensive, evaporating at about 0.5-1% a day, and topped up by truck in a dewar that looked like a scaled-down rocket stage.
children.note: Not established: the 4.2 K figure, the 0.5-1% per day evaporation rate and the truck top-up practice. The helium article confirms that most helium is liquefied by a cryogenic process and that the safety issues resemble liquid nitrogen. The numbers are not in it.

facility.helium.cryo-separation.note: Not established: the -190 C cold box temperature, the 77 K char-bed temperature, the catalytic dehydrogenation and cryogenic adsorption steps, and the 6N (99.9999%) grade. The helium article confirms that the crude gas is purified by successive cooling and that activated charcoal is the final step giving 99.995% Grade-A helium.

facility.water.ion-exchange.name: Demineralisation by ion exchange
facility.water.ion-exchange.description: Strong-acid cation then strong-base anion exchange, then a mixed-bed polish. Removed >95% of the ionic load of the filtered water and got to 10-15 MOhm-cm. It could not remove silica, organics or colloids, and the resin was a huge organic load in itself.

facility.water.mixed-bed.name: Mixed-bed deioniser
facility.water.mixed-bed.description: A single resin bed with the cation and anion beads thoroughly mixed, polishing the effluent of the two-bed demineraliser down to a few tens of parts per billion of the sodium-chloride equivalent. It was the top of the 1980s purity curve and was standard offtake to the wet benches. The resin was regenerated with caustic and acid at the same time rather than in sequence, which is what gave the single-pass polish its quality.
facility.water.mixed-bed.note: Not established: the few tens of parts per billion NaCl equivalent outturn and the 10-18 Mohm-cm resistivity figure. The ion-exchange resin article documents resin types and regeneration but not the mixed-bed polish performance of a semiconductor water plant.

facility.water.ro.name: Reverse osmosis
facility.water.ro.description: Cellulose acetate or thin-film composite spiral-wound elements in 6-inch pressure vessels rejecting 90-99% of dissolved ions, 95-98% of organics and, importantly for the 1980s plant, most of the silica and hardness. The first RO units were installed at plants like this from the mid-1970s. By 1983 they were displacing two beds of ion exchange ahead of the polishers.
facility.water.ro.note: Modern practice is two-pass RO with antiscalant dosing and a final UV and ultrafiltration. The 1980s plant had a single pass and no antiscalant. Not established: the 10-15 bar brackish and 55-70 bar seawater operating pressures and the 95-99.5% salt rejection figures. The reverse osmosis article gives 2-17 bar for fresh and brackish water and 40-82 bar for seawater, and states no rejection percentage.

facility.water.uv.name: UV sterilisation
facility.water.uv.description: A 254 nm germicidal lamp in a stainless vessel, dosing typically 30-40 mJ/cm2, to kill bacteria and oxidise the last of the organics. Added in the late 1980s onward, mostly for the reclaim loop, because a 1970s fab did not sterilise its ultrapure water at all.
facility.water.uv.note: 1948-1983 practice: no UV, no ultrafiltration in most plants; bacteria were managed by keeping the loop hot (60-80 C for hot DI water) or by chlorination upstream.

children.name: Low-pressure mercury lamp
children.description: A quartz envelope with a low-pressure mercury vapour discharge emitting 254 nm, immersed in a quartz sleeve in the water. Same lamp chemistry as the germicidal fittings in hospitals.
children.note: Not established: the 254 nm emission figure and the low-pressure mercury quartz-envelope construction. The germicidal UV article covers lamp dose and EPA dosage guidance but gives the emission wavelength only in an unsourced table template.

facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.name: Nitrogen purge of the air system
facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.description: Before opening a vessel, a line, or a tank that had held flammable or reactive material, it was purged with nitrogen and tested with an oxygen analyser. The purge itself was fed from the nitrogen header or, in a small plant, from a bottled cylinder.
facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.note: Not established: that purging with nitrogen and testing with an oxygen analyser was the 1983 practice before opening a vessel, and that small plants purged from a bottled cylinder. No standard or process-engineering source was located for purge practice of that decade.

facility.water.cooling-tower.name: Induced-draught cooling tower
facility.water.cooling-tower.description: A 20-60 m concrete or steel shell packed with fill, with fan blades in the base drawing air up through the falling film of circulating water. Water evaporates, concentrates the dissolved solids, and is purged to the drain or the recovery plant.

facts.label: Evaporation loss
facts.value: ~1% of circulating flow per 10 C of wet-bulb depression

children.name: Tower fill and eliminator
children.description: Cellulose (Kraft), PVC or polystyrene film fill media in a lattice or dendritic pack, plus a drift eliminator of PVC chevron sheets at the top. Cellulose fill was being replaced by flame-retardant PVC in the mid-1980s for fire reasons.

facility.water.cooling-tower.note: Not established: the evaporation loss of about 1% of circulating flow per 10 C of wet-bulb depression, the 4-8 cycles of concentration figure, and the 20-60 m shell height. The cooling tower cited describes evaporative cooling and drift eliminators but gives none of these figures.

facility.water.evaporative-cooling.name: Evaporative (swamp) cooler
facility.water.evaporative-cooling.description: A finned coil with water sprayed over it and an induced-draft fan. Far cheaper than a chiller in dry climates where the wet-bulb depression is large; marginal in humid coastal sites, where the wet bulb runs high.

facility.water.chiller.name: Reciprocating chiller
facility.water.chiller.description: A compressor, condenser and evaporator in a packaged unit, cooling water or air cooled. The alternative to evaporative cooling wherever the wet-bulb was too high. 1980s chillers were almost all ammonia or R-12/CFC-11, and therefore both a refrigerant-ozone problem and a safety problem.
facility.water.chiller.note: Not established: that 1980s chillers were almost all ammonia or R-12/CFC-11. Modern chillers are documented as vapour-compression units on a separate condenser water loop. The refrigerant mix of the 1980s is not sourced here.

facility.steam.boiler.name: Water-tube boiler
facility.steam.boiler.description: Two-drum or three-drum evaporators with a superheater. Industrial boilers of 4-20 t/h fired coal at about 6-9 bar saturated, directly into the plant's heating and process network. Economisers and feedwater heaters recovered heat. A fraction of the boiler water was blown down to keep total dissolved solids and alkalinity inside limits, which is why the make-up had to be soft or demineralised or the cycles of concentration collapsed. That blowdown went to a flash tank for heat recovery and then to the cooling-water basin. Two spring-loaded safety valves per drum, a feedwater level regulator and a refractory-lined sight-glass port were the bits an operator actually watched.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 2-20 t/h industrial; 50-300 t/h for power-house duty

children.name: Safety valves and drum level control
children.description: Two spring-loaded safety valves per drum, a feedwater level regulator on the drum, and the refractory-lined sight-glass port that operators actually looked at. A steam plant is a place where the concrete is usually older than the manager.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that a safety valve is a fail-safe pressure relief device that automatically releases a substance from a boiler, pressure vessel or other system when pressure or temperature exceeds preset limits; that safety valves were first developed for steam boilers during the Industrial Revolution and that early boilers without them were prone to explosion; and that industry is generally legally required to protect pressure vessels with relief valves under codes such as ASME and ISO 4126. Not established: two spring-loaded safety valves per drum, the drum feedwater level regulator, and the refractory-lined sight-glass port; the source describes the valve type and the legal requirement but states no drum valve count and no level-control arrangement.

facility.steam.turbo-alternator.name: Industrial turbo-alternator
facility.steam.turbo-alternator.description: Where a plant burned coal continuously it made sense to take steam past 300 C and put it through a small turbine to make some of its own electricity. A 2-6 MW pass turbine driving a 480 V alternator, exporting a few hundred kW and buying back the rest at peak rates, was a standard arrangement in Taiwan, Korea and Britain.
facility.steam.turbo-alternator.note: These units were called 'pass turbines' or 'back-pressure turbines' and were the main cogeneration technology before the 1980s gas-engine programme. Natural-gas-fired turbine-generator sets took over from about 1980.

children.name: Speed governor and overspeed trip
children.description: A flyball or hydraulic governor on the turbine shaft plus a mechanical overspeed trip and, in larger sets, a turbine protective device that tripped the generator breaker. The overspeed trip was the last line of defence against a runaway.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that steam turbine governing means controlling the flow rate of steam so as to maintain the speed of rotation; that the throttle governor on small turbines is actuated by a centrifugal governor of flying balls on a sleeve driven through gearing from the turbine shaft, and that larger turbines use an oil-operated servo and relay system; and that every turbine also carries independent emergency governors, or stop actuators, which close the throttle and stop valves and may open a bypass, actuated among other things by loss of control hydraulic pressure or a turbine protection trip. Not established: the mechanical overspeed trip as a named device and the turbine protective device tripping the generator breaker; the source documents the emergency trip function and its triggers but not that hardware line-up.

facility.argon.argon-column.name: Argon recovery column
facility.argon.argon-column.description: A second, smaller column that separates the nitrogen-argon mixture from the top of the nitrogen column into pure argon bottoms and nitrogen tops. Installed when the oxygen plant needed the argon value or the customer paid for it. This was usually in a semiconductor or welding-wire plant, not in a steelworks.
facility.argon.argon-column.note: Partly established: a separate argon column downstream of the nitrogen column, and the high reflux ratio it needs, are documented. Not established: the description of pure argon bottoms and nitrogen tops, and the claim that it was installed in semiconductor or welding-wire plants rather than steelworks.

facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.name: Tube trailer (bulk gas road delivery)
facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.description: A tractor-trailer carrying 30-40 high-pressure cylinders or a single multi-compartment tube bundle of 6,000-15,000 litres, delivering liquid nitrogen, oxygen or argon from a merchant plant. In 1983 this was how a factory without an on-site ASU got its gases. The driver's unload was a vent line that fogged the yard and alarmed the neighbours.
facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.note: Oxygen road tankers in that era were often marked with a diamond placard and were the single most dangerous vehicle in the industrial park. Not established: the 30-40 cylinder or 6,000-15,000 litre capacity, the 2,000-9,000 m3 gaseous equivalent figure, and that this was the 1983 delivery method for a factory without an on-site ASU. No document located on bulk cryogenic road delivery of that decade.

facility.compressed-air.compressor.name: Air compressor
facility.compressed-air.compressor.description: Reciprocating or, from the 1960s onward, oil-injected rotary screw machines. A large electronics plant ran several 100-300 kW screw units. A small sub-contractor ran one 30 kW reciprocating machine under a concrete acoustic enclosure.

children.name: Intake silencer and inlet filter
children.description: An intake filter-silencer combination that kept the machine from eating the dust and the unfiltered outside air. In a coastal site (Kaohsiung, Hong Kong, Long Beach) the sea salt went straight onto the rotors if this was neglected.
children.note: Not established: the sea-salt corrosion mechanism at coastal sites and the intake filter-silencer combination as a distinct item. No document located.

children.name: Drive motor
children.description: A TEFC or, in a corrosive coastal plant, an explosion-proof motor. 400 V three-phase induction motor with a direct-on-line or star-delta starter; speed control only by pole changing.
children.note: Not established: that speed control on a 1983 compressor was by pole changing only, and that explosion-proof motors were used in coastal plants. The induction motor article documents three-phase squirrel-cage drives and TEFC enclosure cooling only.

facility.compressed-air.compressor.note: Not established: the 150-400 kW per machine and 7-8 bar discharge figures, and the claim that oil-injected screw machines were standard from the 1960s onward. The air compressor article documents the reciprocating, vane and screw types only.

facility.compressed-air.aftercooler.name: Aftercooler
facility.compressed-air.aftercooler.description: A water-cooled or finned-air heat exchanger that takes the discharge air from ~100 C down to ~40 C. Without it the machine would not hold pressure in a hot climate and the separator would not work.

facility.compressed-air.separator.name: Water (and oil) separator
facility.compressed-air.separator.description: An automatic drain pot or cyclone knock-out that removes the condensed water and, in an oil-injected screw machine, the injected oil. This vessel was the source of most of the 'the air is wet' complaints in the shop.

facility.compressed-air.dryer.name: Air dryer
facility.compressed-air.dryer.description: Two chemistries in 1983. Refrigerant (absorption or adsorption, e.g. a zeolite unit chilled to 1-3 C) gave a pressure dew point of about 2-10 C, good enough for most pneumatic machinery and marginal for instrument air. Desiccant (two alternating towers of silica gel or molecular sieve with a heatless regeneration on the off-line tower) got the dew point down to -40 to -70 C, which was what a pneumatic logic valve or a moisture-sensitive process needed.
facility.compressed-air.dryer.note: Modern practice is a zero-pressure-change desiccant dryer with a heated purge and dew-point controlled switching. In 1983 the purge air was thrown away, which is why instrument-air plants were noisy and hot. Not established: the 2-10 C refrigerant and -40 to -70 C desiccant dew points, and the claim that the purge air was thrown away in 1983. The compressed air article shows a Joule-Thomson refrigerated dryer on a compressor set. It gives no dew points and says nothing about desiccant units of that period.

facility.compressed-air.receiver.name: Air receiver (accumulator)
facility.compressed-air.receiver.description: A vertical ASME code air vessel, 1-10 m3, acting as a buffer so the compressor could unload on a pressure switch. It also stored enough air to ride through a power cut for a few minutes, which in a fab meant keeping the wet-bench exhaust and the compressors together.
facility.compressed-air.receiver.note: Not established: the 2-10 m3 capacity at 8 bar and the claim that the receiver rode through a power cut for a few minutes. The ASME code vessel is sourced. The sizing is not.

facility.power.cement-kiln.name: Rotary cement kiln
facility.power.cement-kiln.description: A 60-150 m inclined steel tube rotating 1-2 rpm, burning coal or oil at 1450 C to drive off CO2 and drive the reaction forward. Ends at the limestone and clay pits.

facility.steam.fuel-handling.name: Fuel handling and bunker
