facility.steam.fuel-handling.description: A conveyor, a hopper and a boiler feed screw, or an oil tank and a pump skid. Manual barrow-and-shovel coal handling was still normal at plants below about 10 t/h.
facility.steam.fuel-handling.note: Established: that the heat source for a boiler is the combustion of coal, oil or natural gas, per the encyclopaedia article on boilers. Not established: the conveyor, hopper and boiler feed screw line-up, the oil tank and pump skid, and the claim that manual barrow-and-shovel coal handling was still normal at plants below about 10 t/h. The boiler article does not describe fuel handling plant, and no boiler-handling standard or plant survey was located.

facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.name: Cold box (plate-fin heat exchanger)
facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.description: A stack of aluminium brazed plate-fin exchangers, some 10-20 m tall, in which the compressed air is progressively cooled to -196 C by the outgoing oxygen and nitrogen. The heart of every ASU.
facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.note: Not established: the 10-20 m height of the cold box. The air separation article confirms the plate fin brazed aluminium heat exchangers inside a cold box and the 1-2 K approach between the combined condenser and reboiler. The height is not stated.

facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.name: Fractionating columns
facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.description: Insulated stainless-steel columns 5-10 m tall with trays or packing, holding the low-temperature distillation that separates oxygen (bottoms, warmer) from nitrogen and argon (top, colder). A common 1980s arrangement was a single low-temperature column producing oxygen plus a nitrogen-argon mixture, with a side argon column.
facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.note: Not established: the 5-10 m insulated stainless column height and the claim about the common 1980s single-column arrangement. The air separation article documents the high-pressure and low-pressure distillation columns and the 1.2-1.3 bar LP column, not column dimensions.

facility.nitrogen.expander.name: Expansion turbine (expander)
facility.nitrogen.expander.description: A turbine in the cold box that recovers the enthalpy drop of the expanding nitrogen and uses it to generate power, offsetting part of the ASU's compression energy. Standard from the 1960s onward.
facility.nitrogen.expander.note: Not established: that expansion turbines were standard from the 1960s onward and drove the air compressor. The air separation article says modern ASUs use expansion turbines for cooling with the output helping to drive the air compressor. It does not date the practice.

facility.cleanroom.ffu.name: Fan filter unit and laminar flow
facility.cleanroom.ffu.description: A 2.4 x 1.2 m fan-filter unit or a fan coil with an integral HEPA, blowing filtered air down through perforated ceiling tiles at 0.3-0.5 m/s to give unidirectional ('laminar') flow. Open cleanroom used ceiling FFUs over the whole floor. The 1980s move was to a 'minienvironment' (a small FFU box over each process tool inside a Class 1000 room) which was the direct ancestor of today's SMIF pods.

facts.label: Filter bank
facts.value: typically 5-10% of floor area in FFU ceiling

facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing.name: Alkaline scrubber packing
facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing.description: A packed column of plastic Raschig or saddle rings on a support grid, fed with caustic soda or sodium carbonate, stripping acid mist and the base-mist equivalent out of the exhaust. Discharge is a neutral brine sent to the effluent system.
facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing.note: Established by the cited articles: that a packed bed can be randomly filled with small objects such as Raschig rings or with structured packing; that packed beds are used in scrubbers, and that a packed bed performing absorption or stripping is a packed column in which liquid tends to wet the surface of the packing and vapour passes across that wetted surface; and that wet scrubbing uses reagent solutions as well as water to remove water-soluble toxic and corrosive gases. Not established: saddle rings, the support grid, caustic soda or sodium carbonate as the reagents, the base-mist equivalent, and the neutral brine sent to the effluent system; the source names Raschig rings and reagent solutions but no other packing shape, no grid and no discharge chemistry.

facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.name: Incineration of solvent vapours
facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.description: Vapour incineration (afterburner / thermal oxidiser) for the xylene, toluene and trichloroethane vapour from the resist track and the degreaser, plus a wet scrubber or a carbon absorber on the cool side. By the time the air came out it passed an oxidiser at 800-1000 C with a residence time of about one second. The afterburner burned gas or fuel oil, which is what put a burner on the roof next to the acid scrubber.
facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.note: Solvent recovery by activated-carbon adsorption and distillation was increasingly preferred for cost reasons even in 1983. Recovery plant cost money to buy but paid back in solvent.

facility.power.coal-plant.pulveriser.name: Coal pulveriser (mill)
facility.power.coal-plant.pulveriser.description: A ball or roller mill grinds run-of-mine coal to a powder with at least 70% through 200 mesh (75 micrometres) so that it will burn in suspension. This was the technology that made the 1950s-80s boiler possible at all.

facts.label: Mill power
facts.value: 40-70 kW per mill, 2-4 mills per boiler

children.name: Hot-air fan and primary air
children.description: A fan supplies the 60-80% of combustion air that dries and suspends the powder in the furnace and the remainder that sweeps it out between the boiler tube banks.
children.note: Not established: the 60-80 percent combustion-air share for drying and suspending pulverised coal, or that the same air swept the powder between the boiler tube banks on the stations feeding this supply. The split and the duty carry no source.

facility.power.coal-plant.boiler.name: Water-tube boiler and evaporator
facility.power.coal-plant.boiler.description: Drum-type water-tube boiler, typically 300-900 MW, drum at ~15 MPa and 340-370 C. Feedwater circulates through downcomers and up risers around a flame path several hundred passes long. Saturated steam leaves the drum to be superheated. Superheaters raise that saturated steam to 540-565 C by hanging banks of tube bundles in the radiant and convective pass, and reheaters do the same again to the steam coming back out of the high-pressure turbine. Higher steam temperature is the single biggest lever on plant thermal efficiency. An economiser, a bank of finned tubes in the flue-gas path, preheats feedwater from about 120 C to the saturation temperature using the last 8-10% of the flue-gas heat. Ash from the boiler hoppers was quenched, then either dewatered and trucked to a landfill or put wet into a hopper and pumped as slurry. Fly ash was collected in electrostatic precipitators or baghouses and trucked dry or ponded.

facility.power.coal-plant.turbine.name: Steam turbine
facility.power.coal-plant.turbine.description: A multistage expansion turbine: high-pressure, intermediate-pressure and low-pressure sections, the last with the long bladed rotor of a wet-steam half-pressure machine. Exhaust goes to the condenser at about 0.05 bar. Steam rate for a 1980s unit was roughly 9-11 MJ/kWh.

children.name: Surface condenser
children.description: Thousands of stainless-steel tubes with condensing exhaust steam outside and cooling water inside. The condensate is the plant's own feedwater. Cleanliness here directly sets boiler-tube life.
children.note: Established: the surface condenser as a water-cooled shell-and-tube unit condensing turbine exhaust for reuse as boiler feedwater, per the cited article, with stainless steel among the standard tube materials. Not established: the quantitative link from condensate cleanliness to boiler-tube life as stated here.

children.name: Generator (turbo-alternator)
children.description: The turbine shaft turns a 2- or 4-pole alternator at 3000/3600 rpm. A 500 MVA water-cooled unit is about 12 m long and 6 m wide. Output was 13.8 kV or 21 kV. This was far too low to transmit, hence the step-up transformer next door.

children.name: Generator step-up transformer (GSU)
children.description: A single-phase or three-phase bank of 240-500 kV oil-filled transformers that takes 21 kV from the alternator to the transmission line. This is the piece of iron that makes the whole grid possible, and it is why every power station has a lumpy, oil-filled, bunded yard next door.

children.name: Switchyard and circuit breakers
children.description: Outdoor busbars, disconnectors, dead-tank and live-tank oil circuit breakers and surge arresters, on a steel lattice gantry. The step-up point where the plant connects to the transmission network.

facility.power.gas-plant.turbine.name: Gas turbine
facility.power.gas-plant.turbine.description: A compressor, a combustor at 1400-1600 C and a turbine in a single shaft or two. Open-cycle efficiency only 25-35% in 1983. This was the poor number that made gas peakers expensive until combined cycle became standard in the 1990s.

facility.power.oil-plant.boiler.name: Oil-fired boiler
facility.power.oil-plant.boiler.description: Same water-tube boiler as the coal plant, but with oil burners instead of a pulveriser and an induced-draft fan sized for the lower flue-gas volume. Two to four boilers typically share one stack.

facility.power.hydro-plant.turbine.name: Francis turbine
facility.power.hydro-plant.turbine.description: The standard medium-head machine: water enters the spiral casing, turns a runner on a vertical or horizontal shaft at 100-750 rpm, and exits into the draft tube.

facility.coal.washing.name: Dense-medium coal washing
facility.coal.washing.description: Raw coal is floated on a magnetite/water slurry of specific gravity ~1.35. The light coal floats, the ash-rich shale sinks. This is where the mountaintop-removal debate's 'coal refuse' piles come from.
facility.coal.washing.note: Established in general terms by the cited article: preparation plants wash coal of soil and rock and sort it into graded sizes. Not established: the magnetite-slurry specific gravity of about 1.35, the floating-versus-sinking separation as run for this supply, or the mountaintop-removal refuse characterisation.

facility.coal.longwall.name: Longwall face
facility.coal.longwall.description: A mechanised shearer cuts a 2-3 m slice across the panel. The roof is allowed to cave into the goaf and the coal flows to a shearer loader. High recovery, high output, and a lot of subsidence.
facility.coal.longwall.note: Established: longwall extraction across a panel face with roof collapse into the goaf behind, seam thicknesses of order 1-6 m, recovery around 80% (above room-and-pillar), and subsidence as the known consequence, per the cited article. Not established: the shearer-loader flow detail as stated.

facility.coal.room-pillar.name: Room-and-pillar mining
facility.coal.room-pillar.description: Still the dominant method for Appalachian metallurgical and steam coal: rooms driven to the pillar, pillars left behind to hold the roof. Cheap but leaves 30-50% of the seam underground.
facility.coal.room-pillar.note: Established: the room-and-pillar method (rooms extracted, pillars left for roof support) with recovery lowered by the left-behind pillars, per the cited article. Less firmly established: the exact 30-50% left-underground band and Appalachian dominance as stated for 1983.

facility.coal.opencut.name: Open-cut coal mine
facility.coal.opencut.description: Overburden stripped by dragline or shovel, coal ripped by bulldozer, loaded into 100-tonne rear-dump trucks. Dominant in the Powder River Basin, the Ruhr, Limburg, New South Wales and Limpopo.
facility.coal.opencut.note: Established: open-cut extraction by stripping overburden and hauling coal from benched pits, per the cited article. Not established: the 100-tonne truck figure and the claim of dominance in each listed basin.

facility.water.coagulation.name: Coagulation and clarification
facility.water.coagulation.description: Alum or ferric chloride plus lime and a coagulant aid is flash-mixed, then the floc is grown in a flocculation bay and settled out over 2-4 hours in a clarifier. Residual turbidity had to be under about 1-2 NTU for the sand filters to be worth having.
facility.water.coagulation.note: Not established: the 20-80 mg/L alum dose, the 2-4 hour settling period and the under-2 NTU target. The coagulation article supports the mechanism and the role of alum but states none of these figures.

facility.water.multimedia-filtration.name: Multimedia (sand) filtration
facility.water.multimedia-filtration.description: Pressure filters in lead/catalysed iron tanks, 3.5-4.5 m diameter, containing 600-700 mm of graded media. This was typically 100 mm anthracite on 50 mm sand on 25 mm garnet. Backwashed with air scour plus water at 20-40 m/h.
facility.water.multimedia-filtration.note: Not established: the 3.5-4.5 m vessel diameter, the 100/50/25 mm anthracite-sand-garnet bed and the 20-40 m/h backwash rate. No standard or waterworks manual was located stating multimedia filter bed specifications.

facility.water.activated-carbon.name: Activated carbon adsorption
facility.water.activated-carbon.description: A tall bed of coconut-shell, coal or lignite carbon catalytically activated in a furnace, removing humic colour, trihalomethane precursor, pesticide and industrial organics. In the ultrapure plant it was the last chance to remove organics before the ion-exchange resin and the RO membrane.

facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.name: Garment and consumable supply
facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.description: Garments were not laundryable in the era. A hooded coverall was worn once and destroyed. The plant bought enormous quantities of spun-bonded polypropylene garments, hoods, overshoes, gloves, wipes and tacky mats, and washed nothing. One 1980s 5,000-person fab burned something like a million garments a year.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order of 1 million garments per year at a large fab

facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.note: The garment figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate. No published 1983 consumption figure was found. Modern fabs launder and reuse garments and use more reusable materials, which was one of the first sustainability targets in the industry.

facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.name: Acid neutralisation with lime
facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.description: The cheapest and by far the most common treatment: slaked lime or limestone slurry is dosed into a reaction tank, the acid is neutralised, the metal hydroxides precipitate out, and the tank is then settled and the supernatant discharged. It converts an acid into a sludge, which is still a hazardous waste, just a solid one.

children.name: Settling pond / lagoon
children.description: An unlined or clay-lined earthen basin into which treated effluent was discharged and solids allowed to settle, with the supernatant decanted to a stream or a municipal sewer. Thousands of these existed in 1983. The liner requirements came later. The pond was often the plant's cheapest and worst idea.
children.note: Not established: that thousands of unlined settling ponds existed in 1983, and the claim that liner requirements came later is not tied to a dated regulation here.

children.name: Hazardous waste landfill
children.description: In 1983 a hazardous landfill was typically a clay-lined cell with a leachate collection system and groundwater monitoring wells, licensed under RCRA or operating under interim status. Because the Land Disposal Restrictions did not yet exist, most of it received untreated sludge and incinerator ash.

facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.note: No document located that describes lime or limestone neutralisation of semiconductor waste streams as the commonest treatment. The general chemistry is not in question. The claim about frequency of practice in the 1980s electronics industry is unsourced.

facility.power.coal-plant.furnace.name: Boiler furnace and combustion
facility.power.coal-plant.furnace.description: A refractory- and water-wall-lined firebox. Coal and preheated air enter at the burners, burn at 1300-1600 C, and give up radiation to the water walls lining the furnace walls.

children.name: Ljungstrom / regenerative air preheater
children.description: The flue gas gives up its heat to the incoming combustion air through a slow-rotating bank of corrugated steel plates. This is exhaust gas at ~300 C, air at ~300 C. This alone recovered several percent of the coal's energy.
children.note: Established by the cited article: a preheater heats incoming air to raise thermal efficiency. Not established: the slow-rotating corrugated-plate regenerative type, the roughly-300 C gas and air figures, the several-percent recovery, or the 1960-1985 currency for the stations feeding this supply.

children.name: Wet flue-gas desulphuriser (scrubber)
children.description: Required in the US from about 1978 onward once new-source performance standards took effect. Slaked lime or limestone slurry absorbs SO2 to calcium sulphite, which is then forced-oxidised to gypsum. The stack gas is reheated so the plume still rises.
children.note: Established by the cited article: flue-gas desulphurisation removes sulphur dioxide from fossil-plant exhaust. Not established: the post-1978 new-source-standards requirement, the slaked-lime or limestone slurry to calcium sulphite with forced oxidation to gypsum, the stack-gas reheat, or the 85-95 percent removal for the stations feeding this supply.

facility.water.river-intake.name: River or reservoir
facility.water.river-intake.description: Turbid, hard, seasonally variable. The Schuylkill at Norristown, the Sham Chun at Hong Kong, the Tamsui at Taipei, the Keelung river, and the many dams that supplied Hong Kong from the 1960s (Plover Cove, 1973).
facility.water.river-intake.note: Not established: the named intakes and their characterisations. In particular the Sham Chun, Tamsui and Keelung river claims and Plover Cove's 1973 date are not tied to a water authority document here.

facility.hazardous-waste.trichloroethene.name: Trichloroethene (TCE)
facility.hazardous-waste.trichloroethene.description: A chlorinated solvent, 1,1,2-trichloroethene, once the standard vapour-degreasing and wafer-cleaning solvent in the semiconductor industry. A suspected carcinogen; a common groundwater contaminant; the specific reason the Norristown site is on the National Priorities List.

facility.water.well-screen.name: Well screen and gravel pack
facility.water.well-screen.description: Wire-wound or slotted screen with a graded silica-sand or garnet gravel pack, wrapped in geotextile. Stops the well pumping sand and the aquifer silting up the pump.
facility.water.well-screen.note: Established by the cited article: that at the bottom of a well, depending on the formation, a screening device, filter pack, slotted casing or open borehole is left to allow the flow of water into the well; that constructed screens are typically used in unconsolidated formations such as sands and gravels, allowing water and a percentage of the formation to pass through so that a large area filter forms outside the screen; and that such screens are illustrated in stainless steel. Not established: the wire-wound screen type, the graded silica-sand or garnet gravel-pack grading, the geotextile wrap, and the claim about the aquifer silting up the pump; the article names filter pack and slotted casing as alternatives to a constructed screen but gives no gravel grading, no wrap material and no silting mechanism.

facility.cleanroom.access-floor.name: Access floor panel
facility.cleanroom.access-floor.description: A 600 mm square steel or aluminium-frame panel with a steel or cast-iron skin, on adjustable pedestals with seismic and electrical bonding. The panel had to be load-rated for a 1000 kg diffusion furnace cart and still be light enough for two people to lift.

facility.cleanroom.hepa.name: HEPA (absolute) filter
facility.cleanroom.hepa.description: Deep pleated borosilicate glass-fibre media in a galvanised steel casing, rated 99.97% efficient at 0.3 micrometres. This is the most penetrating particle size, hence 'most penetrating diameter'. A 2.4 m x 1.2 m filter was the ceiling module of every 1980s fab, ceiling and laminar-flow bench alike.

facts.label: Media
facts.value: borosilicate glass microfibre on aluminium separator

facility.cleanroom.hepa.note: HEPA rated at 0.3 um is the number quoted then. It is a worst-case penetration figure, not the true 0.5 um count the class designation used.

facility.cleanroom.prefilter.name: Pre-filter bank
facility.cleanroom.prefilter.description: Bag or panel filters (2-5 micrometre) ahead of the HEPA units, on the make-up air ducts and on the return air. The 1980s standard pre-filter was a 5-ply disposable bag of coarse glass fibre in a steel frame, or a V-bank of 1-inch washable aluminium-header panels. It existed because a HEPA that gets loaded with dust is an expensive mistake.

facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.name: Wafer carriers and handling hardware
facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.description: In 1983 a wafer still travelled in a quartz boat inside a plastic carrier, or hand-carried in a PTFE-wafer cassette from process to process. The SMIF FOUP (the sealed nitrogen-purged single-wafer container that made the whole modern fab possible) arrived with SEMI E10 in the early 1990s. Before that, every transfer was an opportunity for a particle, and a large fraction of the total defect budget.
facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.note: Modern practice is the 300 mm FOUP in a minienvironment with automatic material handling. The 1980s practice was a person carrying a cassette.

children.name: Fused-quartz wafer boat
children.description: A slotted quartz holder that carries 25-50 wafers through the diffusion furnace. Fused quartz is used because it survives 1000 C, expands predictably, and is chemically inert to the dopants. Made from high-purity synthetic quartz rod, ground and flame-polished.

facility.hazardous-waste.manifest.name: RCRA manifest
facility.hazardous-waste.manifest.description: A multi-part paper form (the shipping paper, the generator certification and the transporter and facility certifications) carried with the load from generator to treatment, storage or disposal facility, with signed copies returned to the generator. This is the paper trail that later made it possible to reconstruct where Commodore's waste went.

facts.label: Copies
facts.value: at least 4 (generator, transporter, TSDF, and the returned copy)

facility.power.insulator-porcelain.name: Porcelain suspension insulator
facility.power.insulator-porcelain.description: Glazed (glassy) or unglazed (ceramic) insulator strings, 10-20 discs to hold a 230-500 kV line up in the air. Replaced later by composite polymer strings, which is why the classic transmission silhouette disappeared after 1990.

logistics.shipping.containerisation.name: Containerisation (40-foot box)
logistics.shipping.containerisation.description: ISO 40-foot general purpose container: 12.192 m x 2.438 m x 2.591 m internal, holding up to about 32-36 tonnes. One TEU is a 20-foot box. A 40-foot box is two. Box rates had replaced weight rates on the main east-west lanes by the end of the 1970s, so a low-density, high-value cargo like a C64 paid per box rather than per tonne.
logistics.shipping.containerisation.note: The C64 weighed roughly 4 kg boxed. A 40-ft box at 32 t payload would in principle hold hundreds, but in practice the limit was volume and the fact that C64s were not stackable with the packaging of the day, so 250-350 is a working estimate, not a documented figure.

logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading.name: Bill of lading
logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading.description: The negotiable document that made containerised trade possible: a carrier-issued contract of carriage naming the shipper, the consignee, the port of loading and discharge, the freight terms, and the description of the goods. Without it the goods did not move. With it, the bank paid on presentation. The 1983 electronic BOL did not exist. The paper document was the mechanism.

logistics.shipping.import-duty.name: US import duty on a computer in 1983
logistics.shipping.import-duty.description: The C64 entered the United States under the Tariff Schedules of the United States (the TSUS. The HTS did not exist until 1989), classified as an accounting, computing and other data processing machine incorporating a calculating mechanism, item 676.15, dutiable at 5.5% ad valorem. Separately, item 807.00 gave a duty allowance for the US components shipped out for assembly abroad. This for Commodore meant a deduction for the value of the MOS chips and the case shipped to Hong Kong, so only the value added in Hong Kong paid duty.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 5.5% ad valorem (rate confirmed for 1987; 1983 rate not directly verified)

facts.label: Assembly relief
facts.value: TSUS 807.00: duty on full value less US component value

logistics.shipping.import-duty.note: The 5.5% figure for TSUS 676.15 is verified from a 1987 Court of International Trade decision. Not verified: the exact 1983 rate for item 676.15; it is flagged as medium confidence for that reason. Note also that in 1983 the HTS did not exist (it was introduced in 1989) and the Customs Tariff Index, not a searchable database, was the practical reference.

logistics.shipping.customs-valuation.name: Customs valuation and the paper trail
logistics.shipping.customs-valuation.description: US customs value was the transaction value (the price actually paid or payable) which is why Commodore's transfer-pricing between Commodore Electronics Ltd (Bahamas), Commodore Japan Ltd and the Hong Kong branch became the subject of a US Tax Court case that ran from 1991 and shifted $116 million of income between entities. The same transfer prices determined the duty. The documentation for a 1983 shipment would have included a commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading and, in a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal, a certificate of origin.

facts.label: Section 482 adjustment
facts.value: $65.6 M for 1985 and $50.5 M for 1986 added to CBM income

children.name: Commercial invoice, packing list and certificate of origin
children.description: The three documents that travelled with the container besides the bill of lading. The invoice stated the price actually paid or payable, which is the number customs used; the packing list was the count and weight the carrier checked against the manifest; the certificate of origin was what made the 807.00 assembly-relief deduction claimable. In a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal all three had to be issued and retained for years. This is why the tax case could reconstruct Commodore's internal transfer prices two decades later.
children.note: Established by the cited articles: that a commercial invoice in foreign trade is a customs document, used as a customs declaration by the person or corporation exporting, and used to calculate tariffs and international commercial terms; that a certificate of origin attests the goods have met the criteria for originating in a particular country and is the document on which tariffs and other trade measures are based, with a claim for preferential treatment requiring a certificate presented to the customs authority at the port of entry; and that for non-preferential purposes a certificate is often unnecessary while for preferential purposes it is usually mandatory. Not established: the 807.00 assembly-relief deduction and the US tariff context of the early 1980s, the rule that a bonded warehouse or export-processing-zone deal required all three documents to be issued and retained for years, and the claim that the tax case could reconstruct Commodore internal transfer prices two decades later; no tariff schedule or court record was located. The encyclopaedia has no article on packing lists, so the packing list as the count and weight the carrier checks against the manifest rests on no source read here.

logistics.shipping.c64-count.name: Volume Commodore was moving
logistics.shipping.c64-count.description: By March 1983 the C64 was shipping at about 25,000 units a month and had passed the Apple II in monthly unit sales. Roughly half a million had sold in the first six months. At 300 units a 40-foot box, that is about 83 TEU a month. This was about four to five ships' worth of containers a month, which sounds trivial until you remember it was compounding 20-30% a month.
logistics.shipping.c64-count.note: Established by the cited article: that by the end of 1982 the Commodore 64 had already passed the Apple II in monthly unit sales, and that by March 1983 it was being shipped at the rate of 25,000 machines a month. Not established: roughly half a million units sold in the first six months, which the article does not state, and the 300-units-per-40-foot-box packing density. The container arithmetic also does not hold: 25,000 machines a month at 300 to a box is about 83 forty-foot boxes, which is about 42 TEU, so the figure of four to five ships a month is inconsistent with the container-ship article, which counts a 40-foot container as 2 TEU and gives modern ships in the thousands of TEU.

logistics.shipping.ports.name: Ports
logistics.shipping.ports.description: Kaohsiung was Taiwan's largest container port and was ranked the world's fifth-largest container port in 1982. Its first container terminal was built 1969-70 and Container Terminal No. 4 in the Zhongxing Commercial Harbor Area was built from 1983. Keelung, on the northern approach to Taipei, opened the first Taiwanese container ship movements in January 1972 and worked on a filled jetty because of the terrain. Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour terminals, Rotterdam, and Long Beach or Oakland on the US West Coast, plus New York and Newark on the East Coast, completed the set.

logistics.shipping.routes.name: Route times
logistics.shipping.routes.description: Kaohsiung or Hong Kong to Long Beach is about 4,500-5,000 nautical miles via the Luzon Strait and the great circle. At 16-18 knots that is roughly 12-14 days port to port, plus 3-7 days in the terminal on each end. Hong Kong to Rotterdam via the Suez Canal is about 11,000 nautical miles, 22-26 days, with 5-7 days of canal transit and waiting. These were the numbers that set Commodore's inventory position: eight weeks of sea transit each way on the Pacific route, eleven to twelve weeks each way on the Europe route.
logistics.shipping.routes.note: These are order-of-magnitude figures derived from distances and 1980s liner speeds. No published 1983 schedule for a specific Commodore carrier service was found.

logistics.shipping.air-freight.name: Air freight for the high-value parts
logistics.shipping.air-freight.description: Customs values tell the story: a box of 300 C64s entered at, say, $150-200 declared value each would carry $45,000-60,000 of electronics inside a container whose ocean freight was a few hundred dollars. The ICs were the opposite case: a 6510 and a VIC-II at internal transfer value were a tiny fraction of the customs value of the finished case, so nobody flew the chips. The chips came by sea inside the container, and the container moved once. Air freight was for prototypes, for a replacement part in an emergency, and for the tape and the spares.
logistics.shipping.air-freight.note: Air freight in 1983 was priced by weight with a minimum weight, so the economics made it essentially unusable for consumer electronics inbound freight. It was used for sample and prototype shipments and for urgent replacement parts.

logistics.shipping.demurrage.name: Demurrage, detention and the inventory cost
logistics.shipping.demurrage.description: Two separate costs. Demurrage is the charge for leaving a container on the terminal beyond the free time. In 1983 free time was commonly four to five days and the daily charge escalated. Detention is the charge for keeping the container beyond the time allowed at the other end. On top of both sat the real cost: eight to twelve weeks of sea transit each way meant Commodore had to hold inventory in transit and in the destination warehouse, which is exactly the cost structure that rewarded the 'just-in-time' port-to-port discipline and punished Commodore's famous spotty availability in 1983.
logistics.shipping.demurrage.note: Modern practice: much longer contractually-guaranteed free time (7-10 days), published terminal tariffs and time-and-demurrage clauses that convert demurrage into a rental. The published per-day figures quoted today ($65-$315/day at LA/LB) are anachronistic for 1983.

logistics.people.bom.name: Bill of materials (1983 estimate)
logistics.people.bom.description: Brian Dougherty of Berkeley Softworks gave the most-cited contemporaneous breakdown, used as a production cost of $35-50 by 1985: three ROMs at $1 each; eight 64K DRAMs at $1.85 each; SID and VIC-II at $4 each; RF modulator $3; 6510 at $1-2; TTL, buffers, regulators and capacitors together $5; keyboard under $10; PC board $1-2; plastic case $1-2; power supply and connectors $5-10; packaging and manual $1-2. Note what this says: the eight DRAM chips alone were $14.80, more than the case, the board and the modulator combined.
logistics.people.bom.note: These are Dougherty's estimates, not Commodore's accounts. Commodore never confirmed them. The $135 initial production cost is a Commodore figure.

logistics.people.direct-labour.name: Direct assembly labour per machine
logistics.people.direct-labour.description: Roughly 0.5-1.5 person-hours per machine across population, insertion (automated), wave-solder, assembly, test and packing, plus a share of the test and rework. At 1983 Hong Kong and Japanese electronics wage levels of roughly HK$9-14 or JPY 500-700 per hour, that is about US$1-3 per machine of direct labour. This was between 3% and 8% of the $35-50 production cost. Direct labour is genuinely tiny compared with the IC content, which is exactly the point Commodore's vertical integration strategy rested on.
logistics.people.direct-labour.note: Not established: a documented Commodore standard time for C64 assembly. The person-hour estimate is derived from the process steps (insertion is automated; a wave-solder pass plus test plus pack is on the order of 30-60 minutes of attended time) and should be treated as an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a measured value.

logistics.people.hk-wages.name: Hong Kong electronics wages, 1983
logistics.people.hk-wages.description: The Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department's Quarterly Report of Wages, Salaries and Employee Benefits Statistics carried explicit occupational breakdowns for the electronics industry in 1983 (assembler, soldering worker, tester/aligner, quality control operator, packer, machine operator) with average daily wages and normal hours, and it separately flagged that piece rates were common in manufacturing and that the survey therefore reported them on a time basis. Operative daily wages across manufacturing generally sat around HK$60-100 in 1983, so an assembler earned roughly HK$9-14 per hour at a 7-8.5 hour day. Hong Kong had no statutory minimum wage at all in 1983.
logistics.people.hk-wages.note: The scanned 1983 Census and Statistics Department tables are OCR-garbled. The HK$60-100 daily figure is read off the reported range across manufacturing occupations and should be treated as a range, not a single number.

logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.name: Worker at the wave-solder line
logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.description: The single most recognisable job in a 1980s electronics factory. She stood or sat at one end of a 2-3 m wave-solder machine, fed pre-inserted boards into the conveyor, watched for bridging and dry joints, pulled the rejects, and often did the visual inspection and the component-insertion handwork at the same station. Almost always female, usually in her twenties or thirties, on a piece rate or a small hourly premium for yield, and living within an hour's bus ride of the plant in a New Territories squatter village or a public housing block. Hong Kong's 1983 wage survey listed 'soldering worker' as a distinct occupational category for exactly this reason.
logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.note: The 1980s photographs of the Commodore Hong Kong line show a robotised through-hole populating machine followed by a long line with bench test desks, consistent with this description, but they date from December 1992, not 1983.

logistics.people.design-team.name: C64 chip design team
logistics.people.design-team.description: A team of about seven people, working in parallel on two chips, in nine months. Al Charpentier designed the VIC-II with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Bob Yannes designed the SID with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Charles Winterble, then director of worldwide engineering, authorised and managed the project. The whole effort began in January 1981, spent about two weeks studying the Mattel Intellivision, the TI 99/4A and the Atari 800, and finished with first-pass silicon in November 1981 that worked except for one bad sprite. The chips were designed in a modular, deliberately uncompact style (Yannes built one oscillator module and repeated it rather than multiplexing) because design time was the scarce resource, not die area. Neither designer had a modern CAD workstation. Logic was simulated by hand.

facts.label: Team size
facts.value: about 7 (2 designers, 4 draftsmen, 1-2 CAD operators, plus a manager)

logistics.people.design-team.note: Six months is often quoted for this design and the sources do not support it: Charpentier and Yannes both worked the full nine months from January 1981 to November 1981, a figure documented in IEEE Spectrum's 1985 case history and in the C64 design histories. The system-level C64 (architecture on paper in two days, five working prototypes in under five weeks) was a different and much shorter effort by Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki in December 1981.

logistics.people.c64-system-team.name: C64 system design team
logistics.people.c64-system-team.description: After Tramiel decided in late November 1981 that the VIC-II and SID would go into a 64 KB home computer rather than a game console, the machine itself was designed in about five weeks. The architecture was laid out on paper in two days. Five working prototypes were finished just before the new year. The team was Bob Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki, with Yash Terakura of Commodore Japan involved on the Japanese variant. They worked over Thanksgiving and Christmas. Charlie Winterble had set the deadline. Tramiel had decided the machine had to be at the January 1982 CES.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: laid out on paper in two days

facts.label: Prototypes
facts.value: five working units in under five weeks

facts.label: Show
facts.value: January 1982 Consumer Electronics Show, Las Vegas

logistics.people.development-cost.name: Nobody knows what the C64 cost to develop
logistics.people.development-cost.description: Winterble's answer to the question was direct: 'I had no formal budget accountability, other than Jack watching me. Jack said that budgets were a license to steal.' The reason the answer was 'nothing much' is that the fab was not running at full capacity and the design chips were absorbed into existing overhead with no supplier margin at all. Ziembicki: 'We were using people who were there anyway.' Software, per Charpentier, 'wasn't tangible - you couldn't hold it, feel it, or touch it - so it wasn't worth spending money for.'

logistics.people.production-engineering.name: Production engineers who fixed it
logistics.people.production-engineering.description: The unsung labour in Commodore's story: David Ziembicki (production engineer, then Commodore West Chester), Bruce Crocket and Charles Winterble, who had to debug the project and bring it into production, and Robert H. Lane, who became president of Commodore Business Machines Inc in November 1982 and was fired by Tramiel after the June 1983 CES. Kentron's 150 Japanese engineers and technicians (brought in specifically because Commodore Japan's production engineering had worked on the VIC-20) are the documented reason the C64 was eventually manufacturable at all.

logistics.people.qa-defects.name: Labour cost of the quality problems
logistics.people.qa-defects.description: Commodore's labour did not just build machines, it found and reworked other people's mistakes. The 'sparkle' defect was traced after three weeks to a ROM (not the VIC-II) with a pre-charging circuit that was sensitive to a bus contention spike. Three million such ROMs were already in service. A logic error put 64 clock cycles on a scanline instead of 65 and took about five months into production to fix. Assembly-line workers over-adjusted the colour potentiometer until it saturated the colour and wiped out the luma. Electric screwdrivers cut traces on the disk-drive connector, and because those traces went to a connector nobody tested, they passed final inspection. Charles Winterble: 'It takes a very tough person to say I'm not shipping these because they're not as good as they could be - especially when people are clamoring to buy them.'

facts.label: ROMs affected
facts.value: 3 million already in service when the sparkle cause was found

facts.label: Cost of the C64A redesign
facts.value: a substantial redesign was required to fix the Santa Clara build

facility.foundries.corporate-structure.name: Corporate chain that owned all of it
facility.foundries.corporate-structure.description: From the US Tax Court record: Commodore Holding B.V. (Netherlands) at the top; Commodore International Ltd (Bahamas); Commodore Electronics Ltd (CEL, Bahamas) as the principal operating corporation; Commodore Business Machines Inc (CBM, West Chester PA) as the US sales subsidiary and the site of the semiconductor division; Commodore Japan Ltd (CJL); Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd (CE(HK)L) and, after April 1982, the Hong Kong branch of CEL; Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH (West Germany); and CBM International Sales Inc, the DISC. MOS Technology became a division of CBM on 1 January 1981. This is why all the chips were still stamped with the MOS logo until 1989.

facts.label: MOS acquisition
facts.value: CBM agreed to buy MOS in November 1976 for a 9.4% equity stake in CBM; merged into CBM 1 January 1981

children.name: Vertical integration as a strategy
children.description: Tramiel's thesis, and the reason the whole tree looks the way it does: if you own the chip, you do not pay a merchant supplier's margin, you control the schedule, and nobody can raise your price. The concrete results: a $135 initial production cost against a $595 retail price, and a production cost driven down to $35-50 by 1985.

facility.foundries.holding-bv.name: Commodore Holding B.V., Netherlands
facility.foundries.holding-bv.description: The top holding company of the Commodore group. From the US Tax Court record: Commodore Holding B.V. (Netherlands) at the top, above Commodore International Ltd (Bahamas) and the operating corporations. A holding entity, not a factory: it owned, it did not manufacture.
facility.foundries.holding-bv.note: Stipulated facts from the US Tax Court record via the corporate-structure node, not published Commodore accounts; hierarchy per listed order (top, then International, then operating corporations).

facility.foundries.international-ltd.name: Commodore International Ltd, Bahamas
facility.foundries.international-ltd.description: The Bahamian parent of the Commodore group, successor to Commodore Business Machines (Canada) Ltd (dissolved 1976). Financial headquarters in the Bahamas; operational base in West Chester, Pennsylvania (retaining the Commodore Business Machines Inc name for R&D). Owner of Commodore Electronics Ltd.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Bahamian parent, successor to CBM Canada 1976

facility.foundries.international-ltd.note: Stipulated Tax Court facts; successor/siting per Wikipedia Commodore International (1976 reorganisation, Bahamas financial HQ, West Chester operational base).

facility.foundries.electronics-ltd.name: Commodore Electronics Ltd, Bahamas (principal operating)
facility.foundries.electronics-ltd.description: The principal operating corporation of the Commodore group (CEL, Bahamas). Owner of the operating subsidiaries: US sales (CBM West Chester), Japan, Hong Kong, West Germany and the DISC sales arm.
facility.foundries.electronics-ltd.note: Stipulated Tax Court facts; operating subsidiaries owned by the principal operating corporation per listed order (sales, Japan, Hong Kong, Germany, DISC).

facility.foundries.business-machines-inc.name: Commodore Business Machines Inc, West Chester PA
facility.foundries.business-machines-inc.description: The US sales subsidiary and the site of the semiconductor division (CBM, West Chester PA). Owner of MOS Technology (bought November 1976 for a 9.4% CBM stake, merged 1 January 1981; chips stamped MOS until 1989). Operational headquarters where R&D occurred, retaining the Commodore Business Machines Inc name.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: US sales subsidiary; semiconductor division site

facility.foundries.business-machines-inc.note: Stipulated Tax Court facts; MOS dates per MOS node and corporate-structure facts (agreed buy November 1976, merged January 1981).

facility.foundries.japan-ltd.name: Commodore Japan Ltd
facility.foundries.japan-ltd.description: The Japanese subsidiary (CJL). Owner of Kentron Co. (subsidiary October 1982 to June 1986, acquired to fix the C64 and begin mass production January 1983).
facility.foundries.japan-ltd.note: Stipulated Tax Court facts; Kentron subsidiary dates per Kentron node (Tax Court stipulated, not published accounts).

facility.foundries.international-sales-i.name: CBM International Sales Inc (DISC)
facility.foundries.international-sales-i.description: The Domestic International Sales Corporation arm (DISC) for export sales. A sales entity, not a factory.
facility.foundries.international-sales-i.note: Stipulated Tax Court facts; DISC role per corporate-structure description.

facility.foundries.mos.name: MOS Technology / Commodore Semiconductor Group fab, Norristown PA
facility.foundries.mos.description: The fab that made the 6510, the 6567/6569 VIC-II, the 6581 SID, the 6526 CIA and the ROMs. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 by John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin as a second source for Texas Instruments' calculator chips, was majority-owned by Allen-Bradley from 1970, and built its own plant on 14 acres of the Valley Forge Corporate Center, 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania. It was a 1-micron NMOS fab running 4-inch wafers, and it is the only place the C64's silicon came from. None of the five custom chips could ever be second-sourced. Commodore bought MOS outright for a 9.4% stake in CBM in November 1976 and merged it in 1981. The fab was closed in 1992 after Commodore's bankruptcy.
places: 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Montgomery County, Pennsylvania
facility.foundries.mos.note: Sources variously call the location Norristown, Valley Forge or Lower Providence. The EPA documents put the plant at 950 Rittenhouse Road in Lower Providence Township, Norristown PA, in the former Valley Forge Corporate Center.

children.name: Captive fab as a prototyping advantage
children.description: The reason Commodore could design a chip in nine months: the fab was not full, the mask shop and the processing line were on site, and a designer could pull a test chip in a few weeks (or, in an emergency, four days). Ziembicki's line is the whole story of Commodore's speed: 'We were using people who were there anyway... You waste a little bit of silicon, but silicon's pretty cheap. It's only sand.'

facts.label: Turnaround
facts.value: a few weeks; 4 days in an emergency

children.name: After Commodore
children.description: After Commodore the fab became GMT Microelectronics. The fab was bought out of bankruptcy in December 1994 for about $4.3 million plus $1 million of liabilities (including the EPA licence), reopened in 1995, ran a 1-micron process for third parties, and was shut down by the EPA in 2000-01. 183 employees and $21 million of revenue in 1999. It is a rare, well-documented instance of a 1970s fab surviving the death of its owner.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that after the Commodore bankruptcy in 1994 Commodore Semiconductor Group, the successor to MOS Technology, was bought by its former management for about 4.3 million dollars plus an additional 1 million covering miscellaneous expenses including an EPA licence; that the EPA entered into a Prospective Purchase Agreement with GMT Microelectronics in December 1994; that GMT reopened the original circa-1970 one-micrometre process fab in Audubon, Montgomery County, Pennsylvania that Commodore had closed in 1993; and that the site had been on the National Priorities List of hazardous waste sites since October 4, 1989, after a 1978 trichloroethylene leak from an underground concrete storage tank. Less firmly established: the 1995 reopening, where the article gives 1994, and the closure being ordered by the EPA in 2000-01, where the article records only disestablishment in 2001. The 183 employees and 21 million dollars of 1999 revenue quoted here appear in the article without a citation there.

facility.foundries.santa-clara.name: CBM Santa Clara, California
facility.foundries.santa-clara.description: Commodore's US assembly line, where production of the C64 began in late summer 1982. It had automated component-insertion equipment. It went badly: excessive video and audio noise, excessive heat, and semiconductors incompatible with the design, so yield was low, cost high and returns came back. Only a limited number of units came out of Santa Clara before responsibility was shifted to Commodore Japan in the autumn of 1982.

children.name: Automated-insertion board layout fight
children.description: Commodore's US plant used automatic component insertion. The Japanese plant did not, and the two wanted different component spacing. Charpentier's group won: the C64 board was laid out for automated insertion, and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools. This single decision is why every C64 motherboard was made in Hong Kong.

facility.foundries.hong-kong.name: Hong Kong operation (CE(HK)L and the CEL Hong Kong branch)
facility.foundries.hong-kong.description: Where the C64 really got built. Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd had been making watches and calculators since 1979, and manufactured VIC-20 units from April 1982. Later the Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd took over. Mass production of the production-redesigned 'C-64A' began at the Hong Kong branch in March 1983, and that branch employed approximately 2,500 people. Commodore's Hong Kong operation bought or produced watches, calculators and computers, and by 1983 it was the assembly centre for the whole company's output. Commodore had Hong Kong subsidiaries listed as Commodore Business Machines Ltd (Hong Kong) and Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd.

facts.label: Headcount
facts.value: ~2,500 persons at the Hong Kong branch of CEL

facility.foundries.hong-kong.note: The 2,500 headcount and the March 1983 mass-production start are the parties' stipulated facts in the US Tax Court record, not Commodore's published accounts and not industry averages. The exact street address of the Commodore Hong Kong plant is not established in the sources consulted. It is not confirmed as Kwai Chung, Tsuen Wan or Kwun Tong. Photographs of the plant taken in December 1992 by Robert Baker, a Commodore production engineer sent from West Chester PA for the Amiga 600 pilot run, show a robotised through-hole insertion machine, a long assembly/test line and bench test desks.

children.name: Hong Kong PCB fabricator
children.description: All sixteen versions of the C64 motherboard were manufactured in Hong Kong. Hong Kong in the early 1980s was a genuine centre of bare-board fabrication. This was dozens of small plants doing gold-impregnated or tin-lead plated FR-4 double-sided boards on a 0.3-0.4 mm grid with the pads drilled and plated by a subcontractor. Commodore did not own one. It bought them.
children.note: The bare-board manufacturer is not named in any source consulted. 'Manufactured in Hong Kong' is the documented claim.

children.name: Hong Kong / Taiwan injection moulding sub-contractor
children.description: The ABS case, the keyboard keycaps and the cassette-port door were moulded by a sub-contractor, not by Commodore. Hong Kong and Taiwan each had hundreds of small toolrooms and presses in 1983, and Commodore used both. The case cost an estimated $1-2 in 1983 prices.
children.note: The identity of the moulder is not documented in the sources consulted.

children.name: Power supply / transformer sub-contractor
children.description: The linear power supply inside the C64 (the big orange or black transformer, the rectifier and the linear regulators) came from outside suppliers, cost an estimated $5-10 including connectors, and one of Ziembicki's complaints was that a supplier that had passed engineering approval then quietly changed the design without telling anybody.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that an outside supplier provided a power supply for engineering approval, got it approved and then changed the design without telling anybody, in the words of Commodore production engineer David Ziembicki; and that power supply and miscellaneous connectors appear in the parts cost breakdown at 5 to 10 dollars, beside 1 to 2 dollars for the printed-circuit board, 1 to 2 for the plastic case and under 10 for the keyboard. Not established: that the supply was the linear arrangement of a large transformer, a rectifier and linear regulators described here. The source names no internal supply components. The cost figure is also not a Commodore figure: the article attributes the whole parts breakdown to an estimate by Dougherty of Berkeley Softworks, and Commodore would not confirm the cost figures.

facility.foundries.kentron.name: Kentron Co., Ltd., Ina, Japan
facility.foundries.kentron.description: The small Japanese production-engineering company that Commodore Japan acquired in October 1982 and that actually fixed the C64. Kentron had about 150 employees at its height and expertise in production engineering, quality control, work standards, purchasing and materials control. Commodore Japan substantially redesigned the machine into the 'C-64A' with Kentron's help. Kentron produced prototypes in late 1982 and began mass production in January 1983. This was two months before the Hong Kong branch started, which is why Kentron, not Hong Kong, is where the machine was made buildable. Kentron was a CJL subsidiary from October 1982 to June 1986, when it was sold to an unrelated party.
facility.foundries.kentron.note: The acquisition dates and the January 1983 production start are stipulated facts from the US Tax Court record, not published Commodore accounts.

facility.foundries.japan-vendors.name: Japanese assembly vendors for the VIC-20
facility.foundries.japan-vendors.description: The VIC-20 (the machine whose case, board size and BASIC the C64 inherited) was first built in Japan by Shinwa Electric Company, then by Japanese Cash Register (JCR), both assembling and manufacturing to Commodore Japan Limited's specifications and under its direction. Japanese Cash Register also owned a factory on Ina road. CJL's engineering headquarters was at Isaka.
facility.foundries.japan-vendors.note: The C64-Wiki list of Commodore entities includes 'Commodore Japan Limited in Japan (Isaka)'. The Tax Court record confirms Shinwa Electric and Japanese Cash Register as the VIC-20 assemblers but does not give their locations.

facility.foundries.braunschweig.name: Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH, Braunschweig, West Germany
facility.foundries.braunschweig.description: The European production base. Commodore launched production for the European market in Braunschweig in 1980 and it once employed up to 2,000 people. Commodore GmbH also designed products. The PET had been imported from Braunschweig, and Commodore UK in the 1970s bought calculators at a factory on Teesside. After the 1983 Corby decision, the more expensive business systems stayed in Braunschweig.

facility.foundries.corby.name: Commodore Business Machines (UK), Corby
facility.foundries.corby.description: The British end. Commodore UK's head office was in Slough and it built calculators at a factory on Teesside. In 1983 it announced a new GBP 20 million home computer factory at Corby, Northamptonshire, as the European manufacturing and distribution centre for the C64 and VIC-20, expecting 300 jobs by the end of 1984 and 700,000 units a year by then. The Corby plant was in place by September 1984 with 850 jobs on a ten-acre site, ran flat out sixteen hours a day, and was closed as a manufacturing base in January 1986.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: GBP 20 million announced 1983; a little over GBP 2 million of UK grant

facts.label: Jobs
facts.value: 300 planned for 1984; 850 by opening; 170 retained at closure

facility.foundries.corby.note: Corby post-dates the C64's 1983 peak, so it belongs here as the European logistics and finishing node rather than as a 1983 production source.

facility.foundries.other-sites.name: Rest of the manufacturing map, 1983
facility.foundries.other-sites.description: By 1983 Commodore described itself as an international company with manufacturing in Japan, Hong Kong, West Germany, the UK, Pennsylvania and California in the United States, and Scarborough in Metropolitan Toronto. C64 units carried the MADE IN HONG KONG, West Germany or England marks, and were assembled in at least 11 factories worldwide over the model's life. Commodore did not, at this stage, have a Commodore Taiwan plant. The Taiwanese supply chain in this story is the sub-contractor base, not a Commodore factory.
facility.foundries.other-sites.note: The $680 M / 44.7% figure is Commodore's own reported fiscal-1983 sales, not an industry figure, and it is here only because the 1983 annual review is the source for the list of manufacturing countries beside it. Commodore Taiwan as a subsidiary is a later-1980s development. No 1983 evidence of a Commodore-owned Taiwan factory has been found. A Philippine assembly operation definitely existed by the 1990s (the Philippine government seized Amiga and CD32 stock after Commodore's 1994 bankruptcy over a debt to a factory there), but that is outside the 1982-84 window.

facility.foundries.subcontract-network.name: Sub-contractor geography
facility.foundries.subcontract-network.description: Commodore's own factories were few. Its supply base was enormous. Japan supplied the disks and a great deal of the precision mechanics and passives. Taiwan and Korea supplied the display-grade passives, the transformers, the coils, the keyboards and the power supplies, through the export processing zones. The Philippines and Malaysia supplied the switching power supplies and the magnetics by the late 1980s. Hong Kong was the assembly and test node, sitting between them, with the boards printed locally and the chips arriving from Pennsylvania.

facts.label: Hourly compensation index (US=100), electronic equipment
facts.value: 1975: Hong Kong 15-16, Korea 16, Taiwan 18-19; 1984: Hong Kong 19, Korea 23, Taiwan 22

facility.foundries.subcontract-network.note: The wage index here is general, not Commodore-specific: ILO Bureau of Labour Statistics hourly compensation costs for production workers in US SIC 36 electronic and other electrical equipment. It is the cleanest single measure of why the work was in Hong Kong and Taiwan (roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the American cost per hour) but it says nothing about Commodore specifically.

facility.water.pvdf.vinylidene-fluoride.name: Vinylidene fluoride monomer (VDF)
facility.water.pvdf.vinylidene-fluoride.description: Vinylidene fluoride as polymerised to polyvinylidene fluoride ultrapure-water pipe and liner.
facility.water.pvdf.vinylidene-fluoride.note: 170 C melting and no-microbial-growth claims not established per candidate note; R22 pyrolysis to VDF not typed.

facility.water.pvdf.vdf-synthesis.name: Vinylidene fluoride synthesis (R22 leg)
facility.water.pvdf.vdf-synthesis.description: Synthesis of vinylidene fluoride monomer feeding PVDF polymerisation.
facility.water.pvdf.vdf-synthesis.note: R22-derived VDF route per candidate inputs only; conditions not established, type-level step.

facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.felti.name: Coarse glass-fibre melting and felting
facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.felti.description: Coarse glass melted and blown into fibres 100-1000x coarser than HEPA microfibre, felted into a disposable pre-filter mat in a steel frame or V-bank panel.
facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.felti.note: Not established: melt temperature, fibre diameter and binder for the coarse grade; HEPA figures describe the finer borosilicate grade, not this mat.

facility.water.filtered.name: Filtered water (RO/ion-exchange feed)
facility.water.filtered.description: Clarified, multimedia-filtered water feeding the reverse-osmosis unit and the ion-exchange demineraliser: suspended solids, colour and turbidity removed, ionic load still present.
facility.water.filtered.note: Not established: turbidity, SDI or silica figures at the RO inlet; 1980s single-pass practice without antiscalant per the RO note. Operating pressures and rejection percentages stay disowned.

nodes.name: Industrial electricity supply (1983)
nodes.description: The electricity that ran every press, oven, wave-solder machine, conveyor and test rig. In 1983 the world's grids were coal, oil, gas and hydro (not the gas-turbine-dominated grids of today) and industrial customers bought it on a two-part tariff with a demand charge. This node is the utility's own end: the generating stations, the transmission network and the price. The customer's end, from the service drop to the machine tool, is the separate node facility.electricity.
nodes.note: The Taiwan mix figures are the grid that actually powered Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractor base, which is why they are quoted here rather than a world average. Natural gas barely existed as a grid fuel in 1983: the first LNG cargo (Algeria) reached Kaohsiung in 1983 and Hong Kong's town gas came from manufactured coal gas, not natural gas. Established: the node's scope as the utility-side supply (stations, network, tariff). Less firmly established: the exact 1983 price and mix figures, which rest on the three cited datasets.

children.name: Coal-fired steam power plant
children.description: The workhorse baseload of the 1980s. Coal from a mine or a rail/barge unloading dock is crushed, pulverised to talcum fineness, blown into a furnace with preheated air, burned under a boiler, and the resulting steam drives a turbine-generator. Net efficiency typically 33-38% thermal to electricity on a unit built in the 1960s-70s.

children.name: Coal receiving and stockyard
children.description: Unload from rail unit trains or self-unloading barges into a yard. In the 1980s the East Coast plants were fed by unit trains. Japan's and Korea's coal came by Panamax and Capesize bulker.
children.note: Not established: that East Coast plants took coal from rail unit trains or self-unloading barges, or that Japanese and Korean coal came by Panamax and Capesize bulker, for the stations feeding this supply. The delivery modes carry no source.

children.name: Hydroelectric power plant
children.description: Genuinely important for the 1980s Far East: Taiwan took 13.9% of its supply from hydro in 1980 and 24.5% by 1990 (Sun Moon Lake, Tachia, Feitsui, Wujie), and Taiwan's run-of-river stations are exactly the kind of small plant Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors drew from. Elsewhere hydro was the cheap baseload of Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Canada.

children.name: Concrete penstock and headrace tunnel
children.description: A 3-6 m diameter steel or concrete conduit carrying water from the intake at head to the turbine, usually several hundred metres and dropping 50-300 m of head.
children.note: Established by the cited article: a penstock is an enclosed pipe delivering water to hydro turbines. Not established: the 3-6 m diameter steel-or-concrete conduit, the several-hundred-metre length, the 50-300 m head, or the 1960-1990 currency for the stations feeding this supply.

children.name: Tailrace and reservoir
children.description: Where the water goes back to the river. And, downstream of the dam, the river itself is the raw water intake for the industrial park that the dam's power attracted.
children.note: Established: only the term's meaning. This is the channel carrying water away after it leaves the wheel or turbine. Not established: that a downstream river served as the raw-water intake for an attracted industrial park in any particular case. The node makes a generic siting claim.

children.name: Oil-fired steam power plant
children.description: The 1980s default in much of Asia and the Middle East, and the reason Taiwan's grid was 58.8% oil in 1980. Residual fuel oil and fuel oil burned in a boiler instead of coal. This was cheaper to handle, dirtier, and dead on arrival once the 1979 oil shock and OPEC reset prices.

children.name: Tall chimney
children.description: A 150-250 m concrete or steel chimney to get the plume above the inversion layer and disperse sulphur dioxide over a large area. Not a pollution control device. It is a dilution device.

children.note: Not established here: that Taiwan's grid was 58.8% oil in 1980. That figure is quoted with sources on the parent node facility.power. It has not been checked against a primary statistical series for this node. The description of oil-fired generation as the 1980s default in much of Asia is not sourced either.

children.name: Gas-fired power plant
children.description: Two different things share this name. For the 1983 industrial economy the honest answer is that almost none of the grid came from natural gas. Gas turbines ran mainly for peak load, standby and cogeneration. Taiwan's first LNG cargo arrived in 1983 and natural gas did not become a grid fuel until the 1990s.
children.note: In the US the big gas-fired build-out came after 1990, with the EPA NOx rules. In 1983 a gas turbine plant was an unusual and expensive thing to run on a peak-load schedule.

children.name: Nuclear power plant
children.description: Not a 'coal/oil/gas/hydro' machine, but it was 10.2% of Taiwan's electricity in 1980. The first reactor at Chinshan came on line in 1978, followed by further units at Chinshan and Kuosheng through the early 1980s. Any 1983 power bill in northern Taiwan could legitimately be traced to a uranium fuel rod.

children.name: Transmission and distribution network
children.description: High-voltage transmission from the plant's switchyard to the city, then medium-voltage distribution to the industrial park, then the service drop to the customer. This is the piece almost nobody thinks about: roughly 8% of generated electricity is lost in transmission and distribution before it reaches the meter.

facts.label: Transmission voltage
facts.value: 230-765 kV AC, some 500 kV DC by 1983

children.note: Losses have fallen by only a few percentage points since 1983 because the physics of I2R dominates. A modern grid still loses 5-8%.

children.name: Overhead transmission line
children.description: Steel lattice towers or wooden H-poles carrying three phases on aluminium conductor, with shield wires and porcelain or glass suspension insulators. The thermal rating of the conductor, not the voltage, is the limit.

children.name: Utility substation
children.description: Transformer bays, circuit breakers, buswork and the control house that steps transmission voltage down to the 11-34.5 kV distribution level. Utility substations outnumbered the plants. A 1980s industrial park typically had one primary substation feeding a ring of unit substation transformers.

children.name: Medium-voltage distribution feeder
children.description: Overhead or underground 11-13.8 kV feeders with reclosers, sectionalisers and fuses. Underground feeders were standard in the new Hong Kong industrial estates and in Japanese and Korean industrial parks. Overhead was normal in the US outside cities.
children.note: Established by the cited article: distribution substations step transmission voltage down to a medium-voltage band of 600 V to 35 kV, and primary distribution lines carry that medium voltage out to distribution transformers near the customer. Not established: the per-country figures of 11 kV for Hong Kong, 20-22 kV for Taiwan and 13.8 kV for the US, the claim that underground feeders were standard in the new Hong Kong industrial estates and in Japanese and Korean parks, and the recloser, sectionaliser and fuse line-up. None of these is stated in the source read, and no utility document was located for these territories.

children.name: Industrial electricity tariff (1983)
children.description: Industrial customers never paid a simple price per kWh. The tariff was two-part: an energy charge per kWh plus a demand charge per kW of measured maximum demand over a 15 or 30 minute interval. The demand charge rewarded flat load and punished a factory that ran its ovens and its wave-solder line together. Tariff classes ('medium general service', 'large power and light') were negotiated against contract demand and often a five-year commitment.
children.note: Modern practice is the same two-part structure, but with hourly and time-of-use pricing and, in some markets, deregulated retail suppliers. The 1980s tariff was a regulated cost-of-service tariff set by a public utility commission.

nodes.name: Electricity at the factory wall
nodes.description: The chain from the utility's service drop to the machine tool. This is the branch other subsystems should reference whenever they need 'mains power': the substation, the transformer, the low-voltage switchboard, the motor control centre, and finally the cord and plug.

facts.label: Factory service voltage
facts.value: 11-13.8 kV into the plant, 480 V three-phase or 220 V single-phase out of the transformer in the US; 380-415 V in HK/Europe

children.name: Utility service and metering
children.description: A pad-mount or pole-mounted transformer on the utility side of the fence, with revenue metering and a fused cut-out. The customer owned everything downstream of the meter.

children.name: Customer substation
children.description: Where a large factory bought at transmission or sub-transmission voltage: a fenced yard with the utility's metering, an incoming circuit breaker, a main transformer, a secondary switchgear line-up and the plant's own protection relays.

children.name: Distribution transformer
children.description: A laminated silicon-steel core with copper or aluminium windings on pressboard and paper insulation, immersed in mineral oil or Askarel. Oil-immersed units dominated until the 1980s-90s fire codes and the economics of dry-type began to change the picture in Europe and Japan.

children.name: Porcelain bushings and standoff insulators
children.description: Glazed porcelain sheds, cemented with epoxy onto the winding ends, to bring the winding out to a terminal. These are the tall ribbed 'sheds' you see on any pole-top transformer.
children.note: Not established: the epoxy cementing of porcelain bushings onto transformer winding ends. Porcelain and glass insulators are documented for overhead lines. Transformer bushing construction is not covered by the sources read.

children.name: Low-voltage switchboard
children.description: Air-circuit-breaker switchboards at 480/415 V, with bolted busbar, fuses/MCCBs per outgoing way and a transformer tap-selector. Most factory power for small machines was tapped off the board at 120/230 V through a plug.

children.name: Motor control centre
children.description: A vertical lineup of combination starters and contactors with a fused disconnect per motor, feeding the compressors, injection-moulding presses, conveyors and extract fans. The 1980s unit had no variable-frequency drives at all. Speed control was a pole-changing or slip-ring motor.
children.note: Adjustable-frequency drives only became normal in the late 1980s-90s, and the first-generation IGBT VFDs cost more than the motor.

children.name: AC contactors and overload relays
children.description: Silver-alloy contacts on a moulded phenolic base with a shading ring to stop contact chatter, plus a bimetal or electronic overload. The bimetal overload relay, unchanged since the 1920s, was the industrial motor's main protection.

children.name: Power factor correction capacitors
children.description: Motor loads are inductive, so a big factory runs at 0.7-0.85 power factor and gets penalised by the utility. Banks of switched capacitor kVAr corrected it. A capacitor is the cheapest industrial electronics ever made. This is a polypropylene film between two aluminium foils.

children.note: Not established: that factory switchboards were air-circuit-breaker type at 480/415 V with a transformer tap selector, and that small machine power was tapped at 120/230 V through a plug. The switchgear article read does not state board construction or factory voltage practice.

Established: the standard customer-substation function and equipment (transformation between voltage levels, circuit breaker, switchgear, protection), per the cited article. Not established: that any particular plant's yard matched this exact line-up. The node describes a typical yard.

nodes.note: Not established: the factory service voltages quoted in the facts (11-13.8 kV in, 480 V three-phase or 220 V single-phase out in the US, 380-415 V in Hong Kong and Europe). No utility or standards document was located for these values.

nodes.name: Industrial steam plant
nodes.description: Process steam for soldering, cleaning, degreasing, autoclaving and heating the building. Most industrial steam plants of 1983 were coal- or oil-fired package/field-assembled water-tube boilers, often with their own turbo-alternator so that the site exported some of its own electricity.

facts.label: Typical pressures
facts.value: 6-10 bar saturated for process; 25-45 bar / 250-400 C for turbo-alternator schemes

children.name: Boiler house
children.description: A tall, heavily built single-storey steel-framed building with a travelling crane, the boilers in a row, coal bunkers or an oil day tank alongside, and the chimney outside. Even in 1983 it was the tallest building on most industrial sites.
children.note: Not established: the description of the era's boiler house as a tall single-storey steel-framed building with a travelling crane, and that it was the tallest building on most industrial sites. Architectural description, not a sourced claim.

children.name: Steam header and distribution
children.description: A large-diameter steel pipe (300-800 mm) with flanged or socket-welded branches to each user, insulation lagged in magnesium-block or calcium-silicate, and a trap at every low point. Steam was distributed at constant pressure from a header rather than generated at each machine.
children.note: Not established: the 300-800 mm header diameter, the magnesium-block and calcium-silicate lagging practice, and the socket-welded branch detail. No piping or steam-distribution standard was located.

nodes.note: Not established: that most industrial steam plants of 1983 were field-assembled water-tube boilers with their own turbo-alternator, and the 6-10 bar process and 25-45 bar turbo-alternator pressure figures.

nodes.name: Water
nodes.description: Every 1980s electronics and metals plant drank more water than it realised, and it arrived from one of two places. Two distinct demands sit on top of it: ordinary industrial water for cooling, rinsing, process and human use, and, in the fab, water pure enough to grow an oxide on silicon without introducing a defect. Point consumers at facility.water.industrial or facility.water.ultrapure rather than at this node, and attach them with `from`. A water treatment plant is an ingredient of the process, never a component of the product.

facts.label: Industrial process water
facts.value: hundreds of m3 per day for cooling; tens of m3 per day of ultrapure

children.name: Raw water intake
children.description: Either a surface intake from a river or reservoir, or a deep well into a confined aquifer. Surface water for cooling, well water for the ultrapure plant. This is because groundwater is already filtered by geology and low in organics.

children.name: Deep well and well pump
children.description: A 150-300 mm steel or PVC casing to 100-300 m with a deep-turbine or submersible pump. In the Lehigh Valley the sand-and-gravel aquifer gave soft, iron-bearing water that had to be degreased. In Taiwan the wells hit 100-300 m of Pleistocene gravel.
children.note: Not established: the 150-300 mm casing to 100-300 m depths, and the specific claims about Lehigh Valley iron-bearing water and 100-300 m of Pleistocene gravel under Taiwan. No hydrogeological document located for these places.

children.name: River / reservoir intake and pump house
children.description: A screened intake structure with travelling-bar screens, coarse screens and a low-lift pump house on the bank. In practice many 1980s plants (including Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors in the export-processing zones) bought municipal or industrial-zone water from the local authority and paid a tariff, rather than taking their own.
children.note: Not established: that Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors in the export-processing zones bought municipal or industrial-zone water rather than taking their own. No waterworks or government document located on Taiwanese industrial water supply in that period.

The node describes a generic intake choice (surface water for cooling, well water for the ultrapure plant) on the rationale that groundwater is geologically filtered and low in organics. No intake design, capacity, or water-quality figure is established here. The node makes no cited quantitative claim.

children.name: Water pretreatment plant
children.description: Coagulation, clarification, multimedia filtration and activated carbon, all in one reinforced-concrete block that dominated the plant footprint. The purpose is to strip the water of the things that would poison an ion-exchange resin or foul an RO membrane: suspended solids, colour, hardness, chlorine, organics and silica. It feeds both the ultrapure plant and the ordinary industrial side.

nodes.note: Not established: the water volumes. Hundreds of m3 per day for cooling and tens of m3 per day of ultrapure water are not tied to any document for a plant of this size in 1983.

nodes.name: Industrial gas supply
nodes.description: The bulk gases a 1980s electronics plant bought by the tanker load: nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen, plus helium and carbon dioxide.
