Supplied either by an on-site air separation unit, an on-site PSA/membrane/electrolyser, or delivered as liquid from a merchant producer in a road tanker. Everything in this branch except helium and CO2 starts from the same place: atmospheric air.
nodes.note: Attach these gases with from, never children: a nitrogen generator or a tube trailer is an ingredient of a process step, not a component of it. Nitrogen, argon and oxygen are also published as ids other fragments reference directly, so they must keep their names and ids stable. Not established: the 1980s merchant purity specification quoted in the facts (N2 99.99%+, O2 99.5%, Ar 99.99%, H2 99.99%). The air separation article supports ASU output purities of 97.5-99.5% oxygen and co-production of argon, not a merchant-grade table.

children.name: Where hydrogen went in a 1980s electronics plant
children.description: Hydrocarbon and silicone greasing, hydrogen annealing of the copper and the metallisation, the reducing atmosphere in the diffusion furnace and the epitaxial reactor, and (for the tie-in with this story) the hydrogen atmosphere in the case of a lamp or a nickel/plated through-hole fill was not yet standard practice.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that hydrogen is employed in semiconductor manufacturing, to saturate broken or dangling bonds of amorphous silicon and amorphous carbon and so stabilise the properties of those materials. Not established: hydrocarbon and silicone greasing, hydrogen annealing of copper and of the metallisation, the reducing atmosphere in the diffusion furnace and the epitaxial reactor, and the closing remark about lamp or plated through-hole fill; the article documents one semiconductor use and says nothing about furnace atmospheres, about annealing, or about lamp filling.

children.name: Where argon went in a 1980s plant
children.description: TIG welding of the sheet metal and the transformer laminations, the inert blanket over the 1800 C silicon melt in the crystal puller, and (increasingly) argon sputter deposition of the aluminium interconnect in a fab. Almost all of it went into joining metal, not into making silicon.
children.note: Not established: the claim that argon sputter deposition of aluminium interconnect was growing in fabs by 1983, and that almost all argon went into joining metal. Argon is documented as a by-product of air separation. Its 1983 distribution of uses is not.

children.name: 1980s helium shortage
children.description: US Bureau of Mines and then BLM administered the supply. The Cliffside field ran out in the mid-1970s and production was rationed, so helium became genuinely rationed and expensive for laboratories and for leak testing. This is a real constraint on the 1980s helium supply chain, not a later phenomenon.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that after the Helium Acts Amendments of 1960 the US Bureau of Mines arranged for five private plants to recover helium from natural gas and built a 425-mile pipeline from Bushton, Kansas to the government partially depleted Cliffside gas field near Amarillo, Texas, where a helium-nitrogen mixture was injected and stored until needed; and that most United States helium is extracted from the Hugoton gas field area of Kansas, Oklahoma and the Texas Panhandle. Not established: that the Cliffside field ran out in the mid-1970s, that the Bureau of Land Management took over administration, and that helium was rationed and expensive for laboratories and leak testing in the 1980s. The article dates the federal withdrawal of the reserve to 1996 and treats the shortage as a later problem, and no 1980s allocation document was located.

nodes.name: Instrument air and plant air
nodes.description: Every factory ran on compressed air. Instrument air was dried, oil-free air fed to the air-line and to the logic valves. Plant air was for the pneumatic tools, the automated insertion machines and the ejectors. The classic 1980s split was a dedicated compressor for instrument air and one or more dirty machines for everything else.

children.name: Ring main and distribution
children.description: Black steel pipe (galvanised or, better, painted steel) in a ring around the plant with drop-legs to each machine. A ring rather than a spine so that a single closed valve could isolate a section for maintenance. Drops went through a service unit with a tap, a pressure regulator, a filter and a flowmeter at each bench.
children.note: Not established: the 6-7 bar working pressure, the choice of black steel pipe, the ring-versus-spine layout and the service unit (tap, regulator, filter, flowmeter) at each bench. The compressed air article covers moisture in the distribution system, not the piping design.

children.name: Process exhaust (fab wet-bench and furnace)
children.description: A separate, larger system from the instrument air: a scrubbed chemical exhaust ducting the acid, base, solvent and furnace exhaust out of the building, usually to an alkaline scrubber on the roof. The neutral brine it discharges and the metal-bearing sludge it produces are the liquid and solid waste streams of the plant.
children.note: Established by the cited article: that scrubber systems are air pollution control devices used to remove particulates and gases from industrial exhaust streams; that wet scrubbing works by contacting the target compounds or particulate matter with a scrubbing solution, water being the most common solvent for inorganic contaminants although reagent solutions may also be used; that process exhaust can contain water-soluble toxic or corrosive gases such as hydrochloric acid or ammonia which a wet scrubber removes well; and that removal efficiency improves with residence time and with surface area, using spray nozzles, packed towers or an aspirator. Not established: the separation from the instrument air system, the roof-mounted alkaline scrubber, the ducting of acid, base, solvent and furnace exhaust out of the building, and the neutral brine and metal-bearing sludge waste streams; the source describes the scrubbing mechanism but not the fab exhaust layout or the discharges.

nodes.name: Hazardous and industrial waste, 1980s practice
nodes.description: The part of the story usually left out. A 1980s electronics plant generated, per fab, tens of thousands of gallons of spent acid, spent solvent, cyanide-bearing rinse, and metal-bearing sludge a year, plus a smaller amount of contaminated equipment and packaging. What happened to it was loosely governed (in the US by RCRA, which had only been in force for three years in 1983) and often not well.

children.name: RCRA
children.description: The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act became law on 21 October 1976. Its Subtitle C hazardous waste regulations were promulgated 26 February and 19 May 1980 and took effect 19 November 1980. So in 1983 the whole American electronics industry was three years into the most consequential change in waste handling since the Clean Air Act. Generators must determine whether a waste is hazardous, accumulate it in a closed, labelled, inspected area for no more than 90 days, describe it on a manifest, and ship it only to a permitted treatment, storage or disposal facility.
children.note: A regulatory regime, not a thing in the supply chain, hence a note. The 1984 Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments tightened this substantially, including the ban on land disposal of untreated hazardous waste. In 1983 that ban did not yet exist and land disposal of untreated sludge was routine and lawful.

children.name: Ocean outfall
children.description: In the coastal Far East (Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, the Philippines) dilute effluent was and is discharged through a permitted outfall diffuser into the sea, often at a designated ocean disposal zone beyond the territorial limit. The dilution argument is real. So is the fact that the 1980s outfalls had almost no metals monitoring.
children.note: The offshore dumping of raw sludge (not diluted effluent) was also common in the Far East until the early 1990s and was progressively banned.

children.name: Commodore's own solvent site
children.description: The clearest documented example in this whole story. A 250-gallon underground concrete tank at the MOS Technology site at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania (installed with the building in 1970) leaked in 1974. It stored the trichloroethene and other solvents used to clean silicon wafers. MOS replaced it with an unlined steel tank, which leaked too. In 1978 the Audubon Water Company, which supplied the public water system, detected trichloroethene in its wells. PADER concluded by 1979 that the contamination could not be excavated. A ground-water recovery well and a spray/treatment system began in November 1981. An air stripper began in February 1984. The site went on the Superfund National Priorities List on 4 October 1989 and the fab was closed in 1992.

facts.label: Leak
facts.value: 1974; TCE found in public wells in 1978

children.note: The site history is documented in unusually fine detail because it was litigated for 15 years: the tanks, the replacement, the recovery well VFCC-4, the stripper, and the 1981 practice of spraying pumped groundwater onto surrounding fields to volatilise the VOCs. All of that is in the public record.

nodes.note: Established: RCRA as the 1976 US federal hazardous-waste law, per the cited article. Not established: the 'three years in force by 1983' reading (the Act dates to 1976; only the implementing regulations are circa 1980), and none of the per-fab volume figures.

nodes.name: Semiconductor fab building
nodes.description: Where the C64's five custom chips were made. A 1-micron NMOS fab: a raised access floor over a service plenum, a ceiling of HEPA filters feeding laminar-flow hoods and open cleanroom, Class 100 in the process bays and Class 1000 in the support areas, and a yellow-lit room for photolithography. Air changed 100-1000 times an hour and consumed most of the plant's electricity.

facts.label: Class definition
facts.value: Class 100 = <=100 particles >=0.5 um per cubic foot of air

facts.label: Fab capital cost
facts.value: roughly $4 M in 1970 (a small fab) rising through $100-300 M for a full 1980s 100-300 mm fab

nodes.note: The 1980s standard was US Federal Standard 209E (1963), which is why everyone said 'Class 100' rather than ISO Class 5. ISO 14644 only arrived in 1995.

children.name: Raised floor and plenum
children.description: A 600 mm or 900 mm void under a load-rated pedestal floor, with all the process exhaust, the cold water, the nitrogen, the vacuum and the electrical cabling running underneath. The whole architectural idea of the fab is that the floor is a duct. This is also why the 1980s fabs needed full basements and 4.5-6 m ceilings.

children.name: Class 100 and Class 1000 zoning
children.description: Federal Standard 209E Class 100 in the lithography, etch and metallisation bays; Class 1000 in the diffusion, cleaning and packaging areas; Class 10,000 in the corridors, the airlock and the material store. The class was maintained by air pressure differentials (the Class 100 room slightly positive to the Class 1000 room, which was positive to the corridor) which is why the doors of a 1980s fab always felt like they were being blown open.
children.note: Modern practice: ISO 14644-1/2, ISO Class 5 (equivalent to the old Class 100) and Class 7 (Class 1000), with ISO Class 8 corridors and much tighter pressure control.

children.name: Amber (yellow) room
children.description: The lithography bay was lit only through yellow filters (either yellow-lens fluorescent fixtures or, later, a laminated film) so that no light below about 500 nm reached the photoresist. The 1980s specification was that irradiance from 350 to 500 nm should stay below roughly 0.5 W/m2 at the work surface, with the rest of the spectrum unrestricted. Resists of the period were sensitive to the mercury g-line (436 nm), h-line (405 nm) and i-line (365 nm).

facts.label: Actinic lines
facts.value: g 436 nm, h 405 nm, i 365 nm (mercury lamp)

children.note: The classic 1980s yellow room was a room with yellow fluorescent tubes. That alone was often not enough (later measurement work has shown legacy 'yellow' tube lighting can still expose resist within an hour) so good fabs added a second, external filter film. Modern practice is to run the room in white light and rely on the area's low-actinic-UV requirement plus dosimetry.

children.name: Photolithography area
children.description: Mask aligners, coat/develop tracks, bake ovens and the mask storage cabinets. In a 1980s 1-micron NMOS fab the lithography bay was Class 100 with the amber lighting, the operators wore yellow-room coats and face shields, and the photoresist was spun from a solvent (Shipley AZ1350, based on a novolak resin sensitised with a diazonium salt) with xylene or cellosolve acetate.

children.name: Passivation and packaging areas
children.description: Passivation (the final silicon nitride or phosphosilicate glass over the completed aluminium) and then the back-end: wafer probe, dice, die attach, wire bond, and the moulding of the ceramic or plastic package. The back end in 1983 was Class 10000 to Class 1000, not Class 100. The contaminating work (bonding, moulding compound) happened there.
children.note: Not established: that the 1983 back end ran at Class 10000 to Class 1000 rather than Class 100. No standard or manufacturer document was located stating the cleanroom class of a 1980s semiconductor assembly and test area.

children.name: Make-up air and air change rate
children.description: The fab's single largest utility load. Because the Class 100 rooms were almost entirely recirculating, the make-up air was only the leakage plus the exhaust: the acid and solvent fume hoods, the furnace exhaust, the ion-implant exhaust. Even so, a 1980s fab typically ran 100-1000 air changes per hour in the clean bays and 20-60 in the support areas, and the air-handling plant cost tens of millions of dollars and dominated the energy bill.
children.note: Modern practice is roughly the same air-change figure but with far better heat recovery, a 6-second air exchange in Class 1 areas, and much higher total electrical intensity per square foot because the process tools now dominate.

children.name: Temperature and humidity control
children.description: 20-22 C and 40-60% relative humidity, tighter than any other building of the era, and the single most expensive thing in the building to get right. The 1980s control was a system of pneumatic controllers and a mechanical chart recorder. A modern fab uses thousands of sensors and a BMS.

children.name: Gowning and airlock
children.description: A two-stage airlock. It is a 'dirty airlock' for incoming components and personnel in street clothes, and a 'clean airlock' with a cross-over bench for gowning. The costume of the era was a hooded coverall plus boots; in the amber room a yellow-coated garment as well.

children.name: What the building cost (1983 dollars)
children.description: For scale: a small 4-inch fab cost about $4 million in 1970 (about $31 million in 2024 money). A full production fab in 1983 ran from roughly $100 million to several hundred million dollars. National Semiconductor announced a $100 million, 290,000 sq ft plant in August 1983, and UMC spent about $200 million on a 1.2 micron fab in the same year. That is why owning a fab was only ever available to very large firms.
children.note: The $100-300 M figure quoted for a 1980s production fab is right for a 1980s production fab. The $4 M figure is right for an early small 4-inch fab like MOS's, and the two should not be compared without saying which decade and which class of plant is meant.

children.name: Fab workforce, 1980s
children.description: A large 1983 fab ran 5,000-10,000 employees, of whom the majority working on the wafer lines were women. This was the largest single female industrial workforce in many of the regions where the plants went, because the tool operators and the wafer handling were culturally coded as women's work even though they were skilled and tightly controlled.
children.note: Commodore's own Norristown fab was far smaller than a 5,000-10,000 employee plant, so this figure describes the industry-wide pattern and not Commodore. Not verified: a firm headcount for any single named 1983 plant.

nodes.name: Factory and engineering test equipment
nodes.description: Every C64 that left the Hong Kong line had been through a functional test, and the boards had been tested electrically before population and after soldering. In-circuit testers and flying probes were the technology of the era. The automated ATE industry of the 1990s did not exist yet. The capital equipment here was made by the test-and-measurement industry, which is why it is categorised `industry` rather than `assembly`. Assembly is reserved for the operations themselves.

children.name: In-circuit tester (ICT)
children.description: A bed-of-nails fixture pressing 1000 or so spring-loaded probes onto the bare board's pads, measuring resistance, capacitance, diode voltage and, at an increasing share, functional signatures at each node. This was all in a few seconds. By 1983 the analogue resistance-only tester was giving way to the analogue-plus-functional 'in-circuit functional tester' that could catch an unpopulated IC or a wrong-orientation part without a board-level functional test.
children.note: The bed-of-nails fixture itself is bespoke per board revision. This is one of the reasons a new motherboard revision was expensive to introduce and why the 250407 revision mattered.

children.name: Functional tester
children.description: A powered-up test station running a test program from ROM that exercised the VIC-II registers, checked the RAM, drove the keyboard matrix and read back the RAM. On a Commodore line this was a dedicated fixture with a monitor and a keyboard, and the operator's job was to load, run, read the result, box or quarantine.
children.note: Established: the term only. Functional testing is described as black-box testing that verifies whether a system meets its functional requirements, generally ignoring internal program structure, and it tests slices of functionality of the whole system. Not established: a powered-up test station running a test program from ROM that exercised the VIC-II registers, checked the RAM, drove the keyboard matrix and read back the RAM; the dedicated fixture with monitor and keyboard; and the operator procedure of loading, running, reading the result and boxing or quarantining. The article is about software functional testing and says nothing about board-level fixtures, ROM-resident test programs or a Commodore production line.

children.name: Test ROM in the final-test fixture
children.description: A dedicated test ROM (the '501' diagnostic ROM is the one most C64 owners meet) loaded into the machine's own ROM socket during factory final test so the machine could self-test its own RAM, character ROM, CIA timers and VIC registers. It is the same object a user later used to prove the machine worked.
children.note: Not established: that Commodore's factory final test loaded the 501 diagnostic ROM into the machine's own ROM socket, or that the 501 ROM was the diagnostic most C64 owners met. The existence of a 501 test ROM is not in doubt. Its use in final-test fixtures is.

children.name: Burn-in oven and sockets
children.description: A forced-air oven at 70-100 C with burn-in sockets, holding hundreds of boards for 24-72 hours so that early-life component failures (bad solder joints, marginal ICs, leaky capacitors) showed up on the line instead of in the customer's house. Commodore's 1982-83 quality record suggests it was not always run long enough.
children.note: Established by the cited articles: burn-in as the practice of exercising components before they are placed in service, so that certain failures occur under supervised conditions and the components in the initial high-failure portion of the bathtub curve can be replaced; that for electronic components it is frequently conducted at elevated temperature and is also called heat soaking; and that burn-in ovens are built for dynamic and static burn-in of integrated circuits and other electronic devices, in air or nitrogen, in sizes from under ten to over 30 cubic feet, with operating temperatures able to go over 260 C. Not established: the 70-100 C figure and the 24-72 hour duration, the hundreds of boards per oven, and the reading of Commodore 1982-83 quality records as showing the burn-in was not run long enough; the sources state that elevated-temperature burn-in is standard but give none of these numbers, and no Commodore quality document was located.

children.name: Bare-board test and flying probe
children.description: Bare PCB test came first: a bed-of-nails grid fixture to prove every net was etched and plated correctly, catching a shorts-heavy board before it was populated and therefore before the parts were on it. The flying probe (a robot or CNC head with a moving needle that touched nets individually without a fixture) existed by the early 1980s as an engineering diagnostic, and only later became the standard production tester once it got fast enough.
children.note: Today the flying probe has largely displaced the bed-of-nails in production, which removes the per-revision fixture cost. This is a genuine change in the economics of board design between 1983 and now.

children.name: Spring probe and tungsten needle
children.description: The bed-of-nails is a field of sprung tungsten-rhenium or beryllium-copper pins on a 2.54 mm grid, each pressing a few grams onto a pad to make contact. The 1980s fixtures were drilled and wired by hand or on a numerical-control machine from the Gerber artwork, which is why a board layout change meant a new fixture.
children.note: Tungsten-rhenium was the common needle alloy in this era. Beryllium copper became the standard later, and both carry real occupational-exposure caveats for the operators who handled them.

nodes.note: Established: in-circuit (bed-of-nails) and flying-probe testing as the era's board-test technologies, per the cited page. Not established: the claim that an automated test-equipment industry did not exist until the 1990s. Programmable instrument buses date to the 1970s.
